speechtext: That, in accordance with the recommendation contained in their third report, the select standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines be given leave to sit while the House is in session.

of course.

maintopic: COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, CANALS AND TELEGRAPH LINES
speechtext:
I offered my objection to this when the motion was presented in the committee to-day, and I desire to repeat my objection now. My objection is this-and I think it will appeal to the Prime Minister and the government-that we have a very important and large committee sitting while the House is in session, and, as far as I can see, there is no particular rush for the bills that are immediately before the committee. I think that about half of the Canadian National Railway bills passed the committee this morning, and the committee passed several other bills, as the report will show. There has been no delay, in fact everything was done to facilitate the passing of the bills this morning. Under these circumstances, I see no reason whatsoever why this committee should sit while the House is in session. I think that we ought to bear in mind that the privilege of sitting while the House is in session should be granted to a committee only under extraordinary circumstances; that is, when we have a large committee, or when they have an important question to deal with, such as the revision of the Bank

Act last year, or any matter of major importance. The ordinary routine work of a House committee should not occasion the sitting of the committee while the House is in session. Personally, .1 very strongly object to it.

maintopic: COMMITTEE ON RAILWAYS, CANALS AND TELEGRAPH LINES
speechtext:
Many members of the
committee are anxious that the business of the House should be proceeded with as rapidly as possible As my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre knows, it is necessary to have a number of the officials of the Canadian National Railways present at the committee meetings. It is true, a large number of bills were passed this morning, but they were passed largely with the consent of members of the opposition who have been opposing these bills. It would hardly be possible to get through in the two hours in the morning, without taking up a very long time; and in every case the representatives of the railway would have to be asked to come here. I do not think it is' the desire of the government nor of the committee that the work should be rushed any more than is necessary even if this resolution be passed. I think we can have an understanding with the opposition that we can proceed with the bills while the House is in session, so that we can keep the officials of the railway here and continue the work from day to day until it is completed, at whatever time would be suitable for the members of the opposition. I do not think it would be necessary to sit this afternoon, as suggested by the committee, but I think the motion should be allowed to go through so that we can have the officials here to continue the work, instead of calling them for a morning session once or twice a week.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, May 5, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Acting Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Woodsworth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, much has been said in this debate by way of congratulation to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb); but for my part I can find only admiration for his apparent coolness and courage as a messenger in the great surrender of the once great Liberal party. For some time, we have watched the contest waging between the Liberal trenches and the Progressive trenches as to which one of them would be the greater. Here a post office gift, there a breakwater, here a branch line railway, have gained supporters, and we have seen one deserter from the Liberal trench crossing over the aisle, two from the Progressive trench going over to the Liberal trench; but finally illness overtook some of the great warriors on the Liberal line and laid them aside from the fight. Then the white flag was hoisted, and after a consultation between the great leaders, the terms of surrender were accepted by the Liberal party. Or, we might put the matter in nautical language, of which the hon. member
for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) is very fond, and say that the pilot, realizing his difficulties and recognizing the black flag of mutiny being hoisted on his ship, has decided to save his life, has scuttled the great Liberal ship and has taken refuge on the Progressive cruiser; -I may be pardoned for calling the group across the way a party; for, if we accept the definition of that word as given by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), they can hardly be regarded as coming up to that standard; the hon. gentleman's definition of the word " party " given last year was this:
" A party is a' group of men who have decided to advance the public interest along certain lines which they hold in common.'; This is a splendid definition; but if we measure the group across the way by the standard therein stated we cannot come to the conclusion that they are of the full stature of a party. The hon. member for Brome construed the principle of common interest to mean an attit.ude of mind concerning the trade question; while the late member for Halifax said that it was a Liberal mentality towards a reduction in taxes. But if we consider the speeches of hon. members who have composed the group opposite, both in the past and up to the present time-and one might include, if one cared to venture a prophecy, those who may compose it in the future-we can find no common interest actuating the whole party.
It is interesting to note the effect of this budget on different members of the House, and, I think, most interesting of all is the effect that it has had upon the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart, Argenteuil). He at once began to toll the funeral bells of protection and to pronounce its death knell, and in his speech he declared that after having lived in Ontario he could see no signs of industrial prosperity there. Let me inform him that since he left that province there has been a great deal of progress therein; and I should like to cite a bit of history in regard to the industrial progress not only of the province of Ontario but of all Canada. There are four or five points from which it would be well for the House to consider this question. First of all, there is the point of the capital invested in manufacturing. The following table shows the comparative sums invested in the period from 1870, in round figures:

It will be seen what remarkable progress has taken place in the industrial activities of Canada over the period of years I have given. In 1900 there were 14,650 industries employing five or more hands while in 1920 there were 43,200 of these concerns. I need do nothing more than give this table in order to show the remarkable development that has taken place industrially in Canada, and I have no doubt it will be sufficient to disprove the testimony of the Minister of the Interior. I would also remind the hon. gentleman that since he went to Alberta a pitiful change has come over the

situation there. When he left Ontario for that province, Alberta was a land of prosperity; the young men were going from the East to the West, and we all remember how they would return in the winter with money easily won from the fields of Alberta and of western Canada generally, decrying and criticising the young men who stayed at home tugging at the stumps and rocks in these eastern parts. Since the Minister of the Interior has had his guiding hand over that province, sunny Alberta has gone back; but we observe that only one year after his departure from the province, Providence has seen fit to bless that land with one of the finest crops the people have ever had there. I have no doubt therefore that Alberta is praying for his continued absence. The hon. gentleman's knowledge, of the history of the former Liberal party and its relation to the tariff is, I think, about as poor as his knowledge of the industrial growth of Canada: he ascribes all the ills of the country to the high tariff of the Con servative party and says that with the introduction of the low Laurier-Fielding tariff he can see signs of prosperity on the horizon.
Let me deal in a few words with the history of this country in its bearing on the tariff. From 1854 to 1866 we had a reciprocity pact, and there was an agreement between the United States and Canada, or at all events what was known as Canada in those days, that the treaty might be abrogated after one years notice. That notice was given by the United States in 1865, the treaty tvas abrogated in 1866, and there ended' our reciprocity with the country to the south. This reciprocity treaty was ended for two reasons: first, Canadian and British sympathy towards the southern states; and, secondly, the heavy internal taxation of the United States following the Civil War. By this treaty there were reciprocal rights in fishing: Canadians had rights on American shores north of the thirty-ninth degree of latitude, the Americans having rights along the shores of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Cape Breton and other parts of this country. The Americans also had the use of our canals and of the St. Lawrence for purposes of navigation, and there was a reciprocal free admission of nearly all natural products of farm, forest, mine and sea.
Now, I would draw the attention of all parties to this fact, that Canada took no steps to abrogate that Reciprocity treaty. It was generally agreed that Canada had not by any means the best of the agreement, but she was willing to keep her promise and

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
so preserve her national honour. I would also point out that Canada took steps to continue the Reciprocity treaty. In 1865, Galt, the then Minister of Finance, went to the United States and endeavoured to secure a renewal of the treaty; in 1866 he and Howland made another unsuccessful attempt; and even during the years 1866 to 1868 our canals were allowed to be used by the Americans under the terms of the expired treaty. In 1867 the first confederation tariff was put in operation, its maximum rates being from 15 to 20 per cent. In 1869 Sir John Rose, the then Minister of Finance, again renewed the offer to the United States to put in operation the Galt terms of 1865. It is very interesting, in the light of what is said about Sir John A. Macdonald and his " high tariff government," to note that at that very date John A. Macdonald, as he then was, was in the United States endeavouring to get free entry to their markets in return for our fisheries and transportation facilities.
From 1869 to 1873 there was a period of world-wide prosperity, in which Canada had a large share. Unfortunately Nova Scotia alone was suffering, and to her honour and credit be it said that in spite of the disadvantages which handicapped her under confederation she has never been greedy in her demands. In 1874 the Mackenzie government came into power. Now set in one of the worst periods of depression in the history of the country. Industrial depression was prevalent in nearly all other countries, and -while George Brown was in the United States seeking, on the instructions of the Mackenzie government, to secure the restoration of the markets of the United States, Canada was becoming the dumping ground for manufactured products from every other country. It is very interesting to note that while at this time depression was rampant in most countries, the United States was the most prosperous nation in the world. She was extending her boundaries and filling her western lands with endless streams of immigrants. And it is significant that she was protectionist beyond all her rivals. Canada, on the other hand, with her low tariff of 15 per cent, was having serious deficits year after year under the financial administration of Sir Richard Cartwright. In 1878 came into office John A. Macdonald with his National Policy. This was a policy of moderate protection, but always containing-and this is an important point, contradicting the statements made in this House day after day- always containing the offer of reciprocity with
the United States. Not only so, but in 1886 an unsuccessful attempt was made to renew the treaty of 1866, and again in 1891 another unsuccessful attempt was made.
Now I come to 1896, when Sir Wilfrid Laurier was returned to power. His government at once made a further attempt to renew the Reciprocity treaty and open up trade relations with the United States. An embassy was despatched to Washington for [DOT]this purpose, but returned without success, and as a result of this last break-
4 p.m. down Sir Wilfrid Laurier uttered those words which are so well known throughout the Dominion, that "there would be no further pilgrimages to Washington." He then inaugurated what is now known as the Laurier-Fielding tariff, of which the following are the outstanding features,-although (they are often forgotten, notably so by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart)-: First, raising the Canadian tariff to the level of the tariff of the United States,-that sounds very similar to the position we should assume to-day; second, instituting an anti-dumping clause; third, inaugurating a policy of tariff administration, calculated to be just as exclusive in its operation as the tariff administration of the United States was found to be. These were the bases of the Laurier-Fielding tariff. The tariff also included these further points: First, "no further pilgrimages to Washington;" second, no appeal to foreign gods; third, no reduction in tariff; fourth, stability for the business of Canada. These are the strong points of the Laurier-Fielding tariff which brought prosperity to this country.
Now, what happened at that time on the United States side? This brings out a very interesting fact. In 1896 the Republican party gained power and under a strong protective policy established a new high level of tariff rates towards the wh-ole world. The result of that was-and I would draw the attention of the House to this point-that the Laurier government was forced to establish a tariff much higher than any which had heretofore been put in force. So the myth of the Laurier-Fielding tariff being a low tariff is exploded. Theirs was the policy which should be adopted to-day. Included in that tariff was a British preference, thereby gaining for the Liberal party a large increase of English-speaking support throughout the Dominion. The Laurier regime lasted from 1896 to 1911, and under its tariff policy this country, we are told, enjoyed the most prosperous period in its history. But in 1911, at the request of the United States government, Sir Wilfrid

Laurier sought the sanction of the people to a reciprocity agreement with the United States, an agreement which would have given to our neighbours concessions even greater than those which had been asked for in the past. The Laurier government was defeated, and was succeeded by a Conservative government, which, so far as the tariff was concerned, introduced little or no change. In 1922 the Liberal government lowered the intermediate tariff schedules to France and other countries and increased the British preference. Unfortunately Mr. Fielding did not realize that the depreciated currency of those continental countries placed Canadian manufacturers at a great disadvantage.
Now, Sir, in opposition to the declaration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier that there were to be no more pilgrimages to Washington, which he supplemented by a policy of protection higher than that inaugurated by the National Policy of the Macdonald government, the hon. Minister of the Interior asserts that his government to-day is opening the door to American industries, and, in his imagination, has lung the death knell of protection." The Laurier-Fielding protective policy brought prosperity to Canada. The King-Robb-Stewart-Crerar tariff has already brought about lessened receipts in this Dominion of ours, and the funeral bells which they are ringing are deadening the factory whistles of Canada at the present time.
Let us now examine some of the points contained in this budget. There is first the matter of a surplus. Apart from the criticism of that surplus on this side of the House we have the strong stand taken by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Mar-ler) and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), that there is no surplus, and as a party we are quite content to let that idea go to the country, because when a government differ among themselves you may be quite sure that there is something wrong. This surplus that is so often mentioned reminds one of the speech made by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) lately in which he pictured the little boy praying for a toy. We might continue that story and say that the speeches on the other side, following the deliverance of the budget, put one in mind of the little boy after he has got his toy, saying: "I have a toy, I have a toy," for the speeches one after the other continue to repeat: "We have a surplus, we have a surplus." But when they differ among themselves I think that surplus can rightly be considered only a myth.
Second, there is the trade of Canada. There is always something to be said on the matter of our increasing trade, b.ut it is worth study-
ing to see whether or not this increase in trade is worth anything to the country. The imports under the French Treaty mean a lot of money going out of Canada, and nothing coming in. According to our Bureau of Statistics, there is contained in this statement of trade the fact that we have imported half as much whisky and exported twice as much as we did in the two years previous. That, of course, increased our trade, but it did not add very much to the prosperity of our country. I would also draw to the attention of the House that our friends to my left, who are perhaps the strongest supporters of this treaty, have perhaps not studied its results. This budget which has been presented to us is one of "Wait and see." The funeral bells are ringing, and we are told that they will be ringing much louder next year. It is a policy of a hand-out to the United States without any return for us. It is a policy which divides us as a people into classes. It hits one class of manufacturer, but not the others. It. benefits one class, the farmer. Why not other classes? If it is for the advantage of the farmer to get his plough free, why not for the carpenter to get his hammer, and the mason his trowel? This budget illustrates the government's habit of jumping without looking where they are going.

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
The government made the French treaty without a proper study of the situation; it made a Fisheries treaty without a proper study of the situation; it bought a hotel in Paris without a study of the situation and not through a proper representative of this government; and now it makes a tariff without a proper study of the situation.
One point that is strongly emphasized, and which perhaps has brought about this great surrender and the disappearance of the Liberal party in its amalgamation with the Progressive party, is the western situation. On our tariff policy of the past has been laid the blame for all the troubles of the West at the present time, but a careful study of the West will show that there are certain conditions which have hot been sufficiently considered by this House. There is first of all the survey of the West which divides it into sections, half sections, and quarter sections. By that survey the roads were not at all convenient for those living in the West, and1 it clearly prevented community living, which is the proper ideal of agriculture.
There is next the careless farming. If the early settlers of any one of the eastern provinces had farmed in the same way as a great many have done in the West there would be a different story to tell to-day in the provinces of Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The eastern part of this Dominion had just as many hardships to contend with, and I believe more severe ones, than the West has ever had.

speechtext:
It would take all
afternoon to develop the question, but if you will listen for a few moments I will mention one or two. I am very sorry I have not with me at the moment a letter that I received from a very prominent Liberal who is much opposed to this tariff, and who was a former agent of the Liberal government. This letter was written, not by a man simply passing through the West on a train, but by one who had been through all parts of the West, and I will refer to one or two points-there are too many for me to take them all up. The farmers of the East who came here from the Old Country took up their abode on the shores of lakes and rivers. In those days they isolated themselves; there was no possibility of their returning to visit their friends or relations during their lifetime; they absolutely cut themselves loose from their former home ties. But in the case of those easterners who went to the West in the early days-I am speaking of some of my own relations now- they returned to the East each year and spent the winters here living on the easy money they had made and causing dissatisfaction among the people they encountered. But- and that is what this letter in question points out-the careless handling of the land and of implements in the early days of the West resulted in great waste-a greater waste than any tariff will be able to make good. Another point in regard to the western situation was the development there, following prosperity, of land booms and all sorts of frenzied speculation. In the next place there was the adoption of all sorts of fads with respect to taxation. These land booms and foolish forms of taxation have strongly militated against the introduction of capital into the prairie provinces of the West. A point that has been raised in connection with the tariff has been the cry that so much has been done for the manufacturers and so little for the agricultural interests. It may be asked what the manufacturer has received from this country outside of a protective tariff, to which we all contribute our small quota of some eight or ten dollars a head. On the other hand, what have the agricultural interests received from Canada? First of all federal contributions amounting in 1923 to $7,110,500. Towards agriculture Ontario contributes $1,529,000; Quebec contributes $824,200; New Brunswick, $92,912; Nova Scotia, $46,073; Prince Edward Island, $17,621; Saskatchewan, $1,060,975; Manitoba, $664,245; British Columbia, $398,370; and Alberta, $330,000. These sums do not include the grants that have been made by the different provinces towards the construction of colonization roads, a total almost as much as the direct contribution to agricultural development. So that when we compare these two aspects of our life in Canada-and I wish to be fair; I am no more interested in manufacturing than I am in agricultural development-we must admit that our industries have not been the only ones aided.

speechtext: Are not these roads used by cars generally; they are not limited to cars owned by farmers, are they?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In the early history of these colonization roads there were very few cars in use, in fact we might say none at all. To-day almost every farmer has a car, and I am going to speak later on the subject of cars. Instead of destroying industries we should build them up as far as we can believing that they add to the development of the great agricultural interests. Just here there is one point I would like very much to stress. There seems to be a demand in certain quarters for a low tariff. Now, it is very interesting to know that every country with a low tariff is a cheap labour country. The other night the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) spoke of the southern states. Those states were always supporters of low tariff, and it is largely because their vote was absent from congress in I860 or 1866 that the treaty providing for reciprocity with Canada was abrogated. The southern states had Negro or slave labour. They were low tariff communities, and you can set it down as a regular thing that where there is a low tariff there is cheap labour. Do we wish to make Canada revert to the condition of these low tariff countries? I say, no. We have to maintain a different standard of living for our citizens, and I do not think it is in the interest of the Dominion as a whole that Canada should ever become a cheap labour country. I maintain that the budget, instead of considering the public good, has been devised in order to promote the political advantage of the government. Instead of considering all the conditions I have mentioned they have considered only party advantages.
In the budget a reference was made to economy. The government loudly proclaimed the necessity for economy, and that theme has been dwelt upon by several speakers during the present debate. But instead of acting upon their own advice the government have been most extravagant in their expenditures. Instead of placarding the country with notices advising the people to move cautiously the government have shown a bad example by their extravagant outlays. They should have again and again advised the people that the easy-money days were passed and it was time to exercise thrift. Instead of following that course, however, the government have devoted themselves to weakening the industrial position of Canada. They have embarked upon the extravagant 
and unnecessary construction of buildings to the extent of $6,000,000; they have appointed partisan officials at staggering increases in salary; they have made unnecessary additions to the public service. Typical of the latter class is the recent appointment of a Commissioner of Immigration to China. This is one of the acts of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) and illustrates well the methods employed by him in his department. The government have simply capped the climax in the matter of expenditures. They have encouraged feverish expenditures upon, railways, and it is well to recall that this is not a new era inaugurated by them. From 1853 to 1860 the same wild expenditure existed. Ontario was the field of foolish expenditure at that time, as the West is today. In Ontario we had charters and requests for such parallel branches of railway as from Cobourg to Peterborough, Port Hope to Peterborough, Belleville to Peterborough, Brockville to Ottawa, and Prescott to Ottawa, all parallel lines within a few miles of each other. And what was the result?-I am only mentioning these few because they are close to my home, but cases of those kind were found all over Ontario and other parts of Canada. While this form of speculation was going on municipalities were going head over heels in debt under what was known as the municipal loan fund system that was permitted by the provinces. The result of it all was that half of the projects had to be given up. Many of the railways after being started were stopped, because wages rose to a dizzy height, men with contracts gave them up, and the contracts had to be relet at higher prices. The result of all this was that the capital expenditure in these railways became very much higher than anybody expected, and municipalities could not meet the interest and had to default. This old part of Canada received a severe blow, from which we have hardly recovered. The same thing is going on at the present time. Railroads are being built now without any question as to whether they are necessary or unnecessary. There is demand coming from people who have to draw their produce many miles from the market, that a railroad should be built. Even at the present time, with all the railroads we have in the oldest counties in this oountry- Dundas for example-a farmer has to draw his produce a considerable distance. If we take the map and measure straight across as the crow flies we find a distance of eight miles, but the farmers in that locality would have to draw their produce perhaps sixteen miles. In North Renfrew where the distance

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
in a direct line is ten miles, and South Renfrew where the distance is twenty miles as the crow flies, they have to draw their produce twenty-five and thirty miles. In Peterborough county they have to draw eighteen miles. In Bruce the distance to a railway is fifteen miles, in Grey eighteen miles, Peterborough twenty miles, Northumberland twelve, Hastings ten, Addington eight to ten, Lambton fifteen, Frontenac eighteen to twenty miles, Leeds twelve, Grenville twelve. In an old well settled county like Lambton they have to draw their produce fifteen miles in certain parts, and even in the constituency of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) (Argenteuil) they have to draw their produce twenty to tweny-five miles to a market. I am taking the distance to the nearest point of the railway, but we must also consider that these points on the railway are not always market points where a farmer can make a sale of his produce. So that even in this old part of Canada the farmers have to draw their commodities long distances. And yet we are r.ot looking in all cases for a railway to relieve the situation.
In addition to this feverish haste I have mentioned, there is also a lack of energy shown by the government in dealing with very important things that should be dealt with and which should come under this budget. I wish to remind hon. members of the condition that I spoke of in the Speech from the Throne, and that was in reference to continuing the levels along our Great Lakes. This is a very important matter to us in the East. I spoke of it from a health or sanitary point of view, and I wish now to speak of it from an economic point of view. The United States are taking steps to protect themselves, but Canada will be a great sufferer in this matter if the lowering is allowed to go on, unless drastic steps are taken to prevent it. The West will suffer more than any other part of the country that I know of. I do not know whether it is generally known, but it is a fact that the boats coming down through the Great Lakes at the present time are lightering from ten to twenty thousand bushels a trip. Each boat is carrying from ten to twenty thousand bushels less each trip owing to the lessened depth of water in our harbours. That means a great loss to the steamship companies who are not making much at the present time. The lowest loss they are suffering is $675 a trip, but it means also, if it means anything, the very possible increase in transportation rates along the Great Lakes. I know that the government might take the stand, '"What can we do?
114i
We have an International Waterways Commission, now we are going to have two or three other commissions; and what can be done in the matter?" I quite admit that there is no action the government can take to change the physical condition. But we can retaliate, and this is the course that has been adopted all these years in regard to tariffs. How can we retaliate in this matter? We have, I think, two practical methods of retaliation. The first is the closing of our canals. If the Americans persist in the system which is lowering the water level, we can refuse them the use of our canals. Of course some of our steamship companies might suffer if we adopted that course. But there is another alternative. We are to-day the only possessors of several natural resources owned in Canada. One is asbestos, another is mica, another is feldspar, and last, pulpwood.

Yes, and there are others I could name. Here we have in our possession means of retaliation and means of bringing this matter to a head in the United States. But above these methods, I think pulpwood is. the one article that we can hold for retaliation. We are shipping millions and millions of dollars in pulpwood to the United States, and we are not getting very much for it in return. In addition to sending out these natural resources from our own country, we are injuring some of our industries. And speaking of those industries, I would like to draw attention to the position of the newspapers. I have here a letter from a prominent Liberal newspaper, one of the strongest supporters the government have at the present time, the British Whig, published at Kingston. I think, carrying out my idea of some retaliation to prevent the lowering of our waters we might take some stand with regard to pulpwood. The editor of that paper writes to me as follows:

The letter continues :
The mortality list among newspapers since 1914 is appalling, and I do not believe that the concentration of the control of the newspapers of this or any country in a few hands is a good thing for the public. The more freedom that exists in respect to the press the better for the public. Unless some relief is afforded, many another paper will be added to the list of those which have ceased publication.
There is another aspect of the situation which is a very unfair one to Canadian newspapers. I refer to the fact that, whereas we have been obliged to pay 6 per cent sales tax, and from now on a 5 per cent, tax, American newspapers and periodicals are permitted to buy our forest product free of sales tax and return it to this country free of duty to compete with our papers.

speechtext: I may be wrong; I want information; but I have been informed that fine paper was being sold in Canada for, I think, seven cents per pound, and the same paper was being sold' to American users of that class of paper for five cents per pound, irrespective of the sales tax altogether. I may be wrong in that information. I have no hesitation in giving names, and the firm that I refer to was the Howard Smith Paper Company.

speechtext:
Of course, there
are a great many kinds of paper.

speechtext: The same brand of paper.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But there are many brands. That, however, does not offset this statement that our own newspapers are being put out of business by this unfair handling of the pulpwood. I quote further
Thus, they neutralise all our efforts at building up a Canadian national spirit. The peaceful, but no less persistent, infiltration of American ideals thus encouraged, does not make for the good of our nation.
For this and other reasons it might be stated that Kingston papers are requesting total relief from the sales tax on newsprint. May we ask that you give this request your support.
That is a letter which, perhaps, indirectly bears upon the statement that I wish to make, that we have in our hands certain natural resources with which we can retaliate against any steps taken by our neighbours to the south, and the use of our pulp and paper is one that I would very strongly draw

to the attention of the government, so that they may deal with this matter of lowering levels on our lakes which is destroying our Canadian harbours at the present time, interfering very much with navigation, and leading to the very possible increase in rates of transportation.
Before I finish I should like to make reference to a very interesting speech delivered yesterday by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw), In that speech he pleaded with this House that our tariff should be towards the line of free trade. He, curiously enough, and in the interest, not only of the members, but of all Canadians, referred to three countries in the old world which were giving prospects of free trade, and he said that they would be lights on the horizon for us as Canadians. Who do you think were the three countries mentioned by the hon. member. The first was Ireland, the second, Hungary, and the third, Russia. Those were the countries now leading towards free trade, and he would like to draw the eyes of Canada to those three countries. We are more interested in a nation that is very similar to our own in speech, in civilization and in all other ways that one would like to make the comparison, and that is the country to the south. He would like to have drawn our attention to the fact that the United States, as I would gather from his address, was very rapidly approaching a state of free trade. I have here a pamphlet which is called the Tariff Act of 1922 on imports into the United States:
To provide revenue, to regulate commerce with foreign countries, to encourage the industries of the United States, and for other purposes.
So, I say that this is the country we would like to study as they as a people are more akin to us by blood, by language and in many other ways. What is the tariff that they have, this "looking to free trade" tariff which has been spoken of by one or more members. I have a number of points marked in this document, but I do not like to take up the time of the House in referring to them all. This tariff goes as high as fifty and . sixty per cent. In every schedule-and there are 1,400 of them-very particular provision is made that any of the articles brought in will not compete nor interfere in any way with American manufactures. For instance, take the tariff on coal tar products, which is a very extended list of articles and on which the tariff varies. This provision is inserted:
That for a period of two years beginning on the day following the passage of this act the ad valorem

The Budget-Mr. Ross (Kingston)
rate of duty shall be 60 per centum instead of 45 per centum.
There is no possibility of introducing any of those articles into the United States. So, you can go on from article to article through these 1,400 schedules with the ad valorem duty rising as high as 75 per cent on some of them. It is also very interesting to turn to their free list which contains some 200 articles. I should like those hon. gentlemen who are talking about the free trade of the United States just to get this book into their hands, to study the text and the tariff on the different articles, and the special provision made whereby this tariff protects every manufacturing industry in that country. Articles allowed in free include:
Acids; agates, unmanufactured; agricultural implements, provided, that no article specified by name in Title I shall be free of duty under this paragraph.
Here is an interesting item of the free list:
Articles the growth, produce or manufacture of the United States, when returned after having been exported, without having been advanced in value or improved in condition. by any process of manufacture or other means if imported by or for the account of the person who exported them from the United States is admitted free.
There is nothing in the history of tariffs that shows the patience and care taken to protect, even on the free list, the manufacturer, such as that provision. Another article on the free list is:
Barks, cinchona other, from which quinine is manufactured.
None of that is found in the United States, but it is all imported from South America. This is another very interesting provision:
Bolting cloths composed of silk, imported expressly for milling purposes.
There is no possibility of any competition there. This is another very interesting one of the 200 articles of the free list:
Books and pamphlets printed wholly or chiefly in languages other than English.
Does that give any opportunity for competition? Linotypes, typesetting machines, typewriters, sand glass machines, all made in the United States, are free, if there were any possibility of bringing them in; but there is no possibility. This list also includes cobalt and cobalt ore; in fact, every mineral that is allowed in free is an ore, and its free entry is allowed in order to encourage manufacturing. Then we find cocoa, coffee, coins gold and silver, copper and other metal compositions of which copper is a component material, of cheap value not specially provided for. These are free. Also free are
copper ores; and coral, but, observe, uncut and unmanufactured. There is also included in the list one article which hon members would like to know, for the religious benefit of the Chinese in their constituencies. I refer to joss sticks. The House will note with what particular care the United States protect themselves. Minerals are free-but minerals crude, and not advanced in value or condition by refining or grinding, or by any other process of manufacture which is not specially provided for. Then we come to oils, spermaceti, whale or other fish oils of American fisheries, which are all in the list. And here is another very interesting free list: personal effects, not merchandise, of citizens of the United States who die in foreign countries. Quinine and sodium also are free. And last of all is the list in connection with agriculture. In short, there is nothing on that free list in the whole 200 items which would compete with any manufacturing business in the United States. This,
I say, is the country that we should study, and if it is necessary to imitate any country, the United States is the country we should follow. I am not particularly an advocate of imitation, but I certainly say that if there is one nation whose fiscal policy we should copy, and might copy with profit to ourselves, that nation is our neighbour to the south of us. And she is not a low tariff country but one that is well protected.
*One wonders what course one should take for the general good in regard to this matter of tariffs. Many have recommended the appointment of a board; but if such a body would take away from the government its responsibility for the trade policies of this country then I for one would not support it. I believe that the government should be composed of individuals, strong enough to take upon themselves individual responsibility for the management of their several departments and who would not seek to depute that responsibility to any board. If, however, by a tariff board is meant one that would gather information for the use of all classes and groups of people in this country, which information would be readily available at all times, then we can see nothing but good as a result of its appointment. It would be highly advantageous if that board were every day on the job collecting material, gleaning information from all sources for the benefit of the Canadian people. Such information would not be biased politically, would not be coloured by any partisan predilections, and we should be able to have some guidance in the treatment of the question of tariffs.

The Budget-Mr. McMurray
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and the members of this House who have borne so patiently with me this afternoon, and before I resume my seat I would ask the government to take these representations into consideration.
Hon. E J. McMURRAY (Solicitor General):	My apology for rising to address
the House on a subject which has been so widely canvassed already is the fact that I am one of the few Liberal representatives in parliament from western Canada. At the commencement of my observations I wish to associate myself in all sincerity with the feelings, which I am sure all members of this parliament share, of regret at the continued illness of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) which prevents him from occupying his accustomed place in this House and which has made impossible the delivery by him of the budget on this occasion. At the same time I wish to congratulate my colleague the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the exceedingly able budget which he has presented to the House on this the first occasion on which he has undertaken that difficult task. The budget is an epitome of clearness and has proved the business capacity of its author and shown his comprehensive grasp of the situation with which it deals. Rightly, it did not enter into any question of theory but confined itself entirely to dealing with the conditions as they actually existed in Canada to-day. And assuredly it is the duty of a minister of finance, not to speculate on conditions in regard to either free trade or protection but to consider the facts as they actually are and in the light of those facts to submit to parliament such measures as will promote the prosperity and welfare of the people. Judged from that point of view, the budget, I think will find a ready reception at the hands of the Canadian people.
What are the prevailing conditions in Canada? I think it will be readily admitted that our people are suffering from a heavy burden of taxation; and this is true not only of our agricultural communities but of all sections of the country as well. This heavy burden is due in a large measure to the war. The war has disjointed industry in every direction, and that is particularly true so far as agriculture is concerned; for apparently the prices of farm products have been far slower in returning to normal than have , those in any other industry. Agricultural prices have not sc readily stabilized themselves; and apart altogether from any question of extravagance on the part of the farmers in

western Canada, as has been alleged, the outstanding fact is that there have been re-markabfy low prices for all agricultural products as compared with a continuing high level of prices for the things which the farmers are obliged to purchase. The result has been that the large farming population of the country, the people who are engaged in the major industry, find themselves in dire straits, hardly equalled within the last twenty-five years. Indeed, it is questionable whether we can find, in a much earlier period of the country's history, such conditions of hardship as exist in Canada to-day. In the light of these conditions the budget has been drafted. It has been drafted not with any desire to interfere with the protected interest but as a practical measure to relieve the burden of taxation and encourage industry.
The budget is entirely consistent with the Liberal platforms of the past. The platform of 1893 was opposed to protection as a prin ciple and declared:
That the customs tariff of the Dominion should be based, not, as it is now, upon the protective principle, but upon the requirements of the public service.
The platform of 1919 contained a clause declaring the desirability of reducing the duties upon the instruments of production; indeed, it apparently contemplated their entire removal. Another clause pledged the party to lower the cost of living. I submit that this budget is a partial carrying out of these principles. It has been charged by our Conservative friends that the government has struck a bargain with the Progressive party. But I have shown that the budget is entirely in keeping with the party's platforms of 1919 and 1893. I wish this declaration to go out to the country: The Liberal party has made no bargain whatever with the Progressive party. On the contrary, the budget is simply the carrying out, in part, of the Liberal platforms of 1919 and 1893 which I have quoted. In these respects we have been true to the policy and traditions of our party.
The budget is a clear-cut indication that the government is committed to the development of the great natural resources of the Dominion, and affords an opportunity to distinguish between those who adhere to the policy of protection and those who adhere to the policy of a tariff for revenue.
