speechtext: How is it that the hon. gentleman was so positive in 1919?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was not announcing budgets in 1919, neither had I any idea at that time that I would be standing in this House and speaking on this budget.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A great difference.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. I have already said that this budget would be received with great satisfaction by the people. The knowledge that there will be a reduction in taxation of $24,000,000 is good news in the homes of struggling people, to whom a reduction of three or four dollars in taxation is a considerable relief. This reduction in taxation is also very satisfactory to our farming population, who complain that they have been heavily taxed for the benefit of a comparatively small agricultural im-5 p.m. plement manufacturing class, an insignificant class numerically compared with those engaged in agriculture, and even compared with those engaged in manufacturing generally, for all told it numbers only about eight thousand people, with an invested capital of about $94,000,000; a mere fraction compared with the great number of our people employed in agriculture and their capital investment.
Now, what are the arguments of our Conservative friends against the budget? The
only objection that we hear in this House proceeds from those who are in close contact with manufacturing districts. Our Conservative friends never argue the economic justice of protection. We have listened this afternoon to an able speaker, the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross), but not once in the three-quarters of an hour during which he addressed the House did he attempt to justify protection as an economic principle. Protection lays a burden upon one section of the country for the benefit of another section. But our Conservative friends attempt to discount this economic injustice by bringing forward a series of so-called arguments in support of protection. In a word, they are strong in assertion, weak in argument, and lacking in proof. Their first argument is that of the lawyer in court:	They are thinking not of
themselves but of the poor workingman. Invariably the supporters of protection speak about the necessity of providing work for our working people and declare that they should not be obliged to go to the United States and other countries to seek employment. Let us examine the soundness of this argument.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman proceeds, I should like to get him to the point. If he believes that protection is an economic injustice, why does he tolerate it for so many months, why does he not see that it is got rid of at once?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is only one member of the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The rest are fighting
him?
Mr. MeMURRAY: As I have already told my right hon. friend, Rome was not built in a day. One of the evils of protection is that once established in a country it is very difficult to remove it without causing undue hardship not pnly to the working people, whom the Conservatives pity so much in their arguments, but to the country as a whole through the disjointing of business. We are all drawn more or less together in every way, and reforms can only be made step by step.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How, then, does the
hon. gentleman explain the new protection introduced last session for artificial silk?
Mr. MeMURRAY:	My right hon. friend
cannot get over that French treaty apparently.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh no, it is not the French treaty at all, but the budget of last session.

The Budget-Mr. McMurray

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will touch on that.
I wish my learned friend would try and keep to the subject of my argument, instead of wandering afield. *

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: This is keeping to the subject. Do not forget my point.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He was not a member
of the government when that was introduced.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He supported it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I suppose the workingman is not worrying very much about artificial silk to-day at any rate. Now what is the position as to the workingman? The hon. gentleman who has just sat down (Mr. Ross) argued that protection keeps up high prices, and that the workingman gets good wages, possibly the highest wages under protection. It is true that protection will keep up prices to a certain extent, but only to a certain extent, as the history of protection in this country shows. The workingman may get higher wages, but it is debatable whether he gets steady employment or not under protection. He has to pay more for what he consumes just the same, and the financial critic of the opposition was going to benefit the workingman by protecting the farmer and raising the price of the eggs and the cheese and the other things that the workingman eats. He and his friends would put the workingman's employer in a protected market, but is the workingman protected? No, because the doors of immigration stand open, and he must face the competition of those who are coming into this country. He always had had to face that competition in this country, and on more occasions than one employers have come to parliament and urged the bringing into this country of trained artisans, in order as they said, that industry might develop and operate better. So the argument of my Conservative friends that protection is beneficial to the workingman is obviously weak, because he has to buy at a higher price the necessities of life in a protected market and the door is always open to let in immigrants to compete with him. The employer is protected, but the workingman is not. So the argument of our protectionist friends is without foundation.
The second great argument that our protectionist friends make is that protection will build up a home market in Canada. I suppose what is meant by a home market is that there will grow up in this country large industrial centres, giving employment to a large population, which will consume the products that the farmer produces, and in that way supply him with a market for his 
goods, but one thing our Conservative friends have never been able to do is to show just exactly what protection has done for Canada, just exactly how much of a home market it has built up. Australia, for instance, is no great industrial country at all. I would judge from casual reading and the knowledge I have of the large cities of Melbourne and Sydney, that they have grown up without the aid of manufactures or high tariffs. Will my hqn. friends contend that Edmonton, Regina, Vancouver and Winnipeg, cities which have had a phenomenal growth, were built up by protection and by manufactures in those cities? They are distribution centres for a large section of the country, and they would distribute just the same under a low tariff. Goods coming from the United States would develop them just as much, because they are cities that have been built up on the export and import trade passing through. I would doubt very much whether the city of Montreal, which has had a remarkable growth, has not been built up in part by the passing of goods in and out through its doors.
The next great argument of the protectionists, indeed, the favourite one of my right hon. friend and those who follow him, is loyalty to country. We always have had that argument, that the goods consumed in Canada should be produced in Canada by our own people, for our own people. That must be done, no matter what the goods cost, and our protectionist friends charge their opponents with knuckling down to the Americans, with not standing up and fighting them and putting up a high tariff wall. I would ask, who is it that is knuckling down? Who is it that will not stand up and fight the Americans? It is the manufacturer. He asks the agricultural interests to put their shield and buckler out in front of him to shield him. He is the one who is constantly sounding the bugle of retreat; he is the one who will not fight and compete against the Americans. So the argument of knuckling down or backing up goes right home to my hon. friends opposite. They ask the agriculturist to protect and shield the man who is in a position to compete.
Now what has been the real policy of the Conservative party, and have they been sincere in their contentions and arguments? The policy of the Conservative party, as was well stated this afternoon by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross), was laid down by Sir John A. Macdonald on the 7th of March, 1878, in the old parliament buildings here.

The Budget-Mr. McMurray
In concluding his speech Sir John Macdonald said that protection would-
-encourage and develop an active interprovincial trade, and moving as it ought to do, in the direction of a reciprocity of tariff with our neighbours, will greatly tend to procure for this country, eventually, a reciprocity of trade.
Later on, another eminent chieftain of the Conservative party, Sir George Foster, speaking in this House in 1893 said:
But, Sir, if there is anything like honourable reciprocity. anything like reciprocity with mutual advantages, and which can be bought by not paying too dearly from the life blood and industrial blood of this country, if there is any reciprocity of that kind this government stands committed to take it and to strive to get it.
That is the stated policy of the Conservative party. I have often thought, and I believe many others have entertained the same opinion, that the National Policy was a "pick-up" policy. Owing to the condition of hard times prevailing in Canada, a condition that was world-wide Sir John A. Macdonald, astute politician that he was, picked up for the time being a policy of high protection, but he took good care to state that it was to be a moderately low tariff and that its object was, as it ought to be, reciprocity of tariffs with our neighbour to the south. Sir George Foster, as I have said before, emphasized that attitude. When the time came the Liberal party, true to their platform of 1893 brought forth the policy of reciprocity with the United States. In 1911 an election took place on that issue, and where did our Conservative friends stand then? Where did the leader of the opposition stand on that occasion? What was the course of the party who were committed to a policy of reciprocity of tariffs? They opposed reciprocity absolutely in the belief that it would hurt their protegees, the manufacturers of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was the
trouble.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Reciprocity was not going to hurt them but they were afraid it would. So the Conservative party lost courage and trembled at the approach of danger. Reciprocity was in the interests of the people of Canada, as I shall prove by figures before I close, but the Conservatives claimed it meant the insertion of the thin end of the wedge and that although it might be in the interests of the consumers it would injure the manufacturers with whom they are associated and who [DOT] are their political friends. The so-called National policy at its inception failed to visualize the Canada of to-day.' It was evolved when we were a small pioneering people in Ontario, Quebec and
the Maritime provinces and conceived of a market in the towns of the Canada of that day, for the poultry, eggs, vegetable products, and other commodities, which the farmers were able to produce in a small way. That policy never contemplated the great world-wide trade that we enjoy to-day. It never conceived of the great Canadian West with its production of 400,000,000 bushels of wheat a year. If the National Policy had foreseen such a prospect it would never have had the audacity to propose to build up in the manufacturing parts of Canada a home market sufficient to take care of the vast production of the Canada of the future. The National Policy was restricted, it was confined in its outlook, it was not constructive, nor was it really national in its character. It never took into account the development of the vast area of western Canada at all, that portion of our country which to all appearances in the years to come will contain an overwhelming proportion of our population. It took no account of the West, and what did it give to the Maritime provinces? If any section of Canada is entitled to praise for its great loyalty and steadfast adherence to confederation it is those little provinces down by the sea. They maintained this attitude in spite of the hardships they had to encounter, and notwithstanding the fact that they could hardly ever hope to get into the market of central Canada. The only thing I can conceive the National Policy has done for them has been to give them a little protection on coal, and some assistance in the shape of the Intercolonial railway. Why call the policy introduced in 1878 a national policy at all, when it was not national in its character and did not embrace any proportion of Canada? Why call it national when its benefits, such as they were, were confined entirely to a limited section of our people?
Now, let us see what happened in the way of developing Canada as a result of the inauguration of the National Policy? When the National Policy was introduced in 1878 our exports amounted to S67,989,000 and after eighteen years reached a total of $109,000,000, a gain of some forty millions in eighteen years, or 3i per cent per annum. Our imports under the National Policy in 1878 amounted to $90,000,000. In 1896 they had increased to $105,000,000, a gain of fifteen millions in eighteen years or less than one per cent per annum. The total trade of the country increased from $158,000,000 to $215,000,000 in eighteen years, or a growth of l4/s per cent per annum The population from 1878 to 1896 increased one million.

The Budget-Mr. McMurray
Under the Liberal policy adopted in 1896 a different story has to be told.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Was the tariff higher or
lower than previously?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will go into that
whole matter. The tariff was consistently lower. The hon. gentleman may differ with me but I contend that it was lower. I will endeavour to show my hon. friend that it was another policy altogether than the National Policy that made Canada great and prosperous. Under the Laurier policy our exports increased from $109,000,000 in 1897 to 1274,317,000 in 1911, or a growth of 120 per cent in that period, at least three times the rate of growth under the National Policy. The imports were more marked than that. O.ur imports increased from $106,000,000 in 1897 to $452,725,000, or 327 per cent in 1911, or at the rate of over twenty-three times what they were under the old policy, and our total trade in those fifteen years increased from $230,000,000 to over $727,000,000, or at the rate of nearly fifteen times what it was under the old National Policy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What was the tariff on
agricultural implements in 1897?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will give my hon.
friend all that later if he will allow me to develop my argument. The population of Canada in these fifteen years increased by two and a quarter million. I well remember in Ontario a portion of the time when the National Policy was in operation. Those were dark and dismal days in our country. Our people were leaving Canada by the thousands. The National Policy could not supply employment for them at home. The young Canadian, the manhood of Canada, went to the States, to build up Chicago and Detroit, to populate Minnesota, the Dakotas and Montana. Prices fell in the country. I well remember my father selling milch cows, good quality, at $18 and $20 apiece, and horses at $50 apiece. I boarded in Stratford with a man who worked for $1 a day shovelling coal. Wages fell. The market was not in Canada. It had reached its full development. They could employ no more. There was no more market. The Conservative party never had the capacity, or the National Policy never had the capacity, to settle the Canadian West.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Did the Conservative
party have anything to do with the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Conservative
party probably had something to do with the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway to the West, but if the Conservative party

were not favourable to settling the country, Canada would be better without the road if that party were to remain in power. While they may have started the construction of that road, my hon. friend would probably be frightened if I were to recite the circumstances of the connection of the good old Conservative party with the building of that road. We know what happened in Canada in the eighties. Our people went out of this country. The many statistics that I have before me will show that native-born Canadians were going out of Canada at the rate of 116,000 to 120,000 a year, and that was not at a time or under conditions such as exist in Canada to-day. During the war, while Canada was wasting its blood and treasure, the United States was accumulating tremendous amounts of money and was gathering together vast stores of wealth that had to find an outlet in the development of the resources of that country, calling to our artisans in Canada to go over there. It is not to be wondered at that there would be an emigration from this country to the United States under those circumstances. These are exceptional circumstances in the country. But when that great emigration went from this country to the United States during the fifteen years of the National Policy, there were no such differential circumstances between this country and the United States. The two countries had great natural resources to be developed, and they were populated by a race of people very much akin, but the National Policy could not keep the people on the farm, and could not give work to the people in the city. Wages were low and prices were poor. They could not develop the country and Canada was in a very serious predicament. Had there not been a complete change of policy by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government, had they continued merely the National" Policy, the great Canadian West would never have been settled, and we in all probability would have been in a serious condition financially.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
W'hat policy did
they give us?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will tell my hon.
friend the policy they gave us, and I will also answer the questions asked by the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol). They gave us a great immigration policy, a policy that opened up the doors of the great Canadian West to the people of the country. The Conservative party had absolutely nothing to give to the West, never gave anything to it and never would. They cannot show in all the years they were in power in this country a single thing they gave to the West.

The Budget-Mr. McMurray

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They gave the people the railway to get there.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They gave them the railway? That railway was first started by the Liberal government under Alexander Mackenzie.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To what extent did the
Laurier tariff increase or decrease customs duties, particularly with reference to agricultural implements which you have been discussing?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have it all right here. The firsi thing that the Laurier government did when it came into office was to look over the resources of this country, and proceed with their development. One of the first things that government did was to establish a cold storage system to take care of the products which the farmer had to sell in his home market. The National Policy had failed to establish a home market. It could never have dreamt of establishing a home market as its advocates prophesied to the people of Canada. A home market might have been established for a small section of Canada where they were producing in a limited way; but taking this country with all its great resources, the National Policy was one of restriction, one of walking slowly, something that might have developed this country in thousands of years to come, but which never could have developed Canada in any reasonable time. Things had to be brought into the country in order to build it up. Outside markets had to be established. The goods-of the country had to go out of the country, and, as one hon. gentleman said the other evening, when you sell your goods you must be prepared to buy. The Liberal party established a great cold storage system, and they commenced to lower the rates on the railroad. The Crowsnest pact was established at that time to protect the farmers of western Canada in the rates they had to pay. They did reduce the duties my hon. friend speaks of. The duties were reduced all along the line in 1907 on agricultural implements.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was asking about 1897.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The condition of this
country at that time by reason of the National Policy was such that there was a positive danger if too active and drastic action were taken. We simply had to take things as we found them and carry them along; and true to our pledges, we turned to reciprocity and reduced the tariff all along the line in 1907. Four years later we proposed reciprocity with
the United States, and, true to our policy, we fought it out. There is a suspicion, and more than a suspicion, abroad in this country, that vast capital was gathered together of those interests who were not being injured at that time at all by the reciprocity pact, to fight for their own selfish advantage against the welfare of the vast consuming and producing population of this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Under the reciprocity pact, was not the tariff on all agricultural implements, everything the farmer has to buy, and particularly cement, much higher than the tariff is to-day?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Then 'I will ask the
hon. gentleman: Why did he vote against reciprocity? Why did the Conservative party oppose it if those tariffs were higher as he alleges? Is there any consistency in their attitude?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I asked if that was not a fact. It is no answer to ask another question.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a very fair answer.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is the usual Scotch
method.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The method is well
recognized.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does my hon. friend want an answer to his question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I may say that I opposed reciprocity because it was placing on the free list everything the farmer had to produce and nothing he had to buy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My hon. friend's views, apparently, were at great variance with those of the farming population of this country in that regard.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We find, however, in 1907 a substantial reduction all along the line on articles from what they were in 1894 and very much from what they were in 1883. If my hon. friend will pardon me, I will come in due course to the question of reduction of those duties.
The immigration policy of the Laurier government, carried on in spite of the high tariff conditions in which we found ourselves, brought into Canada in fifteen years 2,250,000 people; it multiplied our trade by 500 per cent; it multiplied our imports by more than

The Budget-Mr. McMurray
that amount, and it found for the manufacturing interests of this country a market that their Conservative friends could not find for them at all. In those fifteen years the great cities of the West grew, the cities of Ontario grew, Montreal grew, Vancouver grew; they grew because of a great immigration policy, arvd they proceeded to develop the resources of this country and to open it up.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was this immigration not owing to the fact that railways had been built through the western country enabling the country to be settled? In the earlier days of the National Policy, those railways were not there and consequently the country could not be settled.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Those railroads were
there for a long time. The Canadian Pacific was built through in 1882, 1884 and 1885. The country was there and just as rich as it is now, just as rich as Montana, just as rich as the Dakotas, to which the National Policy was sending 100,000 to 125,000 of our young Canadians every year to settle and populate that country. Why could the National Policy not have sent those young men to western Canada? It could not do that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They were all scared that the Liberal party were going to bring in free trade.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They are not very
much afraid of it now. In western Canada the people have never been afraid of free trade. It was that immigration policy that built up the very city which my hon. friend has the honour to represent. What the manufacturers of this country want is a home market for themselves. The producing people, the agriculturists of Canada, can never have a home market of any adequate size supplied to them here. They must go out to the world with their supplies. The great failure of the National Policy was that it destroyed the home market for the manufacturers. My hon. friends have asked me concerning the reductions in the duty on agricultural implements, and it is very interesting to consider the attitude of manufacturers of agricultural implements from the day of Sir John A. Macdonald's tariff, his so-called National Policy, to the present time. I say without fear of contradiction, that manufacturers of agricultural implements in this country have been opposed to or, at least, have never demanded a high protection policy. I have the examination of Mr. Aost, of the Frost and Wood Company, held before a committee of this House away back in 1876. He was asked whether his company wanted protection. He was asked this question:

How does the cost of material, rent, and labour in the United States compare with the cost in Canada?
He replied:
The machine we sell at Prescott at $75, twelve months credit, is sold by the American manufacturers at Ogdensburg, at $100.
Q. Still you sell cheaper than the manufacturers in the United States?
A. Yes, 25 per cent. By competition we succeeded in driving them all out of the country.
John Watson of Paris, Ontario, a well-known manufacturer there, giving evidence on the same occasion, said:
I have worked up my business, commencing with two men up to what it is to-day, increasing each year. Just as my capital increased I put it in the business.
Then he was asked this question:
If we adopted a policy which would require protection to iron manufacturers as well as other trades, the effect of that would be injurious to your trade?
A. Yes; I think our business is protected just as much as it is necessary to protect it. The Americans can do nothing in the way of sending their goods here. We can compete with them in any shape, and we produce an article which they cannot excel.
Mr. SUTHERLAND): What was the tariff at that time?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was 15 per cent. Then Mr. Watson was asked this question:
Do you believe the policy of the present government in not protecting home industries is a good policy, allowing the Americans to flood our market with goods?
A. I think it is better to do that than to increase the tariff-
And I would call the attention of my hon. friends opposite to this.
-because the foundation of this country is agriculture and if you increase the tariff for the benefit of manufacturers, of course it must be disadvantageous to the farmers. I have noticed that in a season when the farmers were prosperous the better position they were in, the better position I was in.
And, the better position that the agriculturists of western Canada, indeed of Canada as a whole, are in, the better for the manufacturers of this country. They should cultivate the home market, not destroy it. I have this letter, dated in 1876, from Mr.* Massey of the Massey-Harris Company. In conclusion, he says:
We may also add that the existing tariff is satisfactory to us-
It was 15 per cent at that time.
-and is sufficient protection, perhaps even a little less would also be. A still further advance in the tariff would certainly prove adverse to our interests.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not want to disturb my hon. friend, but I should really like to know what they got in 1897.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

Never mind disturbing me; I shall probably disturb you before I

am through. I will tell my hon. friend what they got in 1911.

speechtext:
This was the evidence of Mr. Metcalfe, of the International Harvester Company, given before the committee of Ways and Means in the United States. He was asked the following questions:
Mr. Cumpacker: Do ydu manufacture any cheaper in Canada than in the United States?
Mr. Metcalfe: They do not.
Mr. Cumpacker: As cheaply ?
Mr. Metcalfe: Comparatively.
Mr. Cumpacker :Can you manufacture cheaper than the English manufacturer or the German manufacturer ?
Mr Metcalfe: I think they can, otherwise they could not compete with them in Germany and England.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
During the course of my remarks this afternoon, possibly at the risk of being exceedingly wearisome to the House, I produced a considerable quantity of figures which I assert substantiate the proposition that high protection, as established under the National Policy by Sir John A. Macdonald, was not a national policy at all, as it was confined to a very small area of the Dominion of Canada, practically to the province of Ontario and a small portion of the province of Quebec, and had not considered the great Canadian West, and had nothing to offer to the Maritime provinces. I maintain that those figures prove that that policy failed lamentably to advance our trade, that it failed to hold our population, that our people went by the thousands and hundreds of thousands to the United States, that during that time prices had fallen, that the National Policy was incapable of supplying the labouring men with work, that it absolutely failed, as it must do, to provide a home market in a country of vast natural resources such as Canada possesses, and that it was not fair to the farmer, consumer or the working man. I endeavoured further to prove, in dealing with the facts and figures of the 15 years of the Liberal regime under Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that Canada had advanced with wonderful rapidity, had become known to the world as a great exporting and trading nation by reason of the well-founded and active immigration policy introduced by Sir Clifford Sifton, that
the National Policy was incapable of setting or developing western Canada, that the prosperity that existed and the success achieved in manufacturing in eastern Canada during that time were due largely to the fact that an aggressive policy of immigration had developed a home market for the manufacturers, and that instead of, as my hon. friends the Conservatives argue, a market being required for the agriculturists and those producing natural resources, what is really required is a home market for those who must manufacture.
I further asserted, and still assert, that the Conservative party have never been sincere in their protestations of a desire to obtain reciprocity with the United States. It is true that their outstanding leaders have asserted in the past that reciprocity was their aim and that they should endeavour to procure it at the earliest possible moment; but in 1911, when the field was open, and the Americans had a reciprocity treaty on their statute book, our friends showed their true colours and rejected reciprocity. I claim, Sir, that reciprocity would be a good thing for Canada. Following the dark and dismal days immediately preceding the year 1854, the period from 1854 to 1865 was one of wonderful prosperity in the development of Canada's trade and production. I am fair enough in my argument to admit that there were certain exceptional circumstances to encourage the development of the great natural resources of Canada at that time. There were the Russian and American wars, but still in spite of that Canada had no such prosperity except such as she later enjoyed under the Laurier regime. It is interesting to have the figures before us, and I take the liberty of placing them upon Hansard. To show how great an extent Canada's export trade with the United States increased under free trade-1854 to 1866-I give the following figures:

In the face of that showing, because of the fear that artificially protected interests always have of any attack which might be made upon them, the manufacturers of Canada and the Conservative party turned down reciprocity. In the face of those facts every person conversant with Canadian affairs will realize that, with reciprocity in force, the result would have been tremendous in the development of trade and the progress of Canada.
I have always endeavoured to prove that our manufacturers, if they had the courage, are quite capable of going out and competing with the Americans across the border, or as a matter of fact, with all the other countries of the world. I may say that we shipped out of this country into the United States a considerable quantity of manufactured articles. In 1910 the manufacturers of agricultural implements in Canada were shipping $86,000 worth of goods to the United States. At the same time they were shipping to the other countries of the world nearly $5,000,000 worth. It was at that time my right hon. friend, the leader of the opposition made his argument in this House that by reason of the big export trade with these other countries, the factories of Canada were quite capable of standing on their own feet with a small protection because they were able to go out into the world and compete. The farmers of Canada were paying for protection to the consumers of another country. If that be true in 1910, with $5,000,000 of an export trade, it is doubly true to-day when they export over $812,000 to the United States and $9,339,519 to other parts of the world. That clearly proves that they are quite capable of standing on their own feet, if the argument of the leader of the opposition was good in 1910, and we in the West are absolutely sure that it was a sound and reasonable argument at that time.
There are within our country many manufacturers who can stand on their feet without any protection at all; for instance, the great pulp and wood industry, the paper manufacturing industry, the flour industry, with our splendid electric power and in a country that produces a vast quantity of cheap food. There is no reason whatever why this country cannot compete successfully with the United States. I have before me a list of statistics dealing with the manufacturers of Canada. In 1922-23 we exported to the United States $248,988,128 worth of manufactured and semimanufactured goods from Canada. The particularly interesting thing about this from the point of view of my argument is that fully 11a
or chiefly manufactured goods to the amount of $135,521,437 were manufactured in Canada and shipped by Canada to the United States.
During last summer we had the interesting experience of having the leader of the opposition come to western Canada and we are particularly proud of him in that western country. We look upon him as one of our own there. He was with us for a long time and after 1910 when he made that speech on "The ramparts of gold and the Chinese wall," we were quite prepared to take him to the bosom of the West as one of our own. He came to the West this year. Conditions were bad and he told us that they were very bad in all parts of Canada. The picture that he painted to us was a gloomy one, and then he prescribed a remedy. The Conservative party is a real, genuine Conservative party in its remedies. It is like the old time doctor who had but one remedy which was to bleed; bleed the patient on all occasions. When our good friend the leader of the opposition came to western Canada this year, he prescribed for our ills his one and only remedy, the remedy of the Conservative party, the remedy of Macdonald, Foster and the leader of the opposition. He told our farmers and the people generally in western Canada that they wanted high protection.

Mr, McMURRAY:	The right hon. gentleman will have to give me credit; I may have misread him. I naturally thought that would be his argument. I knew it was not his argument in 1910. He was then a western man; but since then a great deal of water has flowed under the bridge and my right hon. friend has grown closer to those in the Conservative party. I have heard a great deal of high protection talk during this debate, and I presume it is in keeping with the right hon. gentleman's opinions on that question. At any rate, it seemed to produce a feeling like a cold breeze throughout the prairies. It seemed as if the wind had swung away north over the Hudson bay again. The farmers put their overcoats on and turned up their collars. He had with him on that occasion the great Sachem, Ferguson*, from the dominant province of Ontario, and he evidently talked high pro-

The Budget-Mr. McMurray
tection. He was going to benefit the good old province of Ontario by having them consume the coal of Alberta. It did not matter if that coal was going to cost them three or four dollars more a ton, it was to be hauled over all the distance from Alberta to Ontario and laid down there at a high price. That was honesty; that was real, genuine protection; but I feel that the people of Ontario would not welcome the application of that form of protection which we have enjoyed in western Canada for so long.
The people of western Canada, as I alleged this afternoon, have received no benefit whatever from the National Policy. The home market has not been able to take a fraction of what they produce. This is the proof that the home market has not succeeded. In the days of the McKinley tariff, disaster fell upon Canada. There was no market for the farmers' products. The home market had not developed. When the Fordney tariff was imposed upon cattle, that industry perished in western Canada. There was no home market for it. Our capacity to produce from our great natural resources is so tremendous that a home market idea is something of a terrible joke. So it is that the people of the West in regard to many of these industries feel that they are like Sinbad the Sailor. The old man of the sea is on their backs; they have carried him a long while; he has booted them in the ribs, and they will be glad to be relieved of that burden.
What is to be the future development of our western country? Sometimes my hon. friends of the Conservative party, in a moment of forgetfulness, state their true thoughts upon this question. I have before me the smiling face of the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens). In the Listening Post in April, he is dealing with conditions in western Canada and I read with marked interest his very able statement. I considered it able, because we always think anything is sound and solid that agrees with our own views. He was talking of that magnificent city of Vancouver and the fine province of British Columbia. The article is headed "The Outlook for the Pacific," and the hon. member modestly stated:
During the year 1923, there has been exported by deep-sea shipping from British Columbia 550,000,000 feet of lumber which is approximately double that of last year, and about ten times what it was eight years ago.
In addition to this, he says, it is evident that large quantities have been exported by rail to the United States and eastern Canada. He says that there has been exported through the port of Vancouver between September 1 and March 1 29,429,000 bushels of wheat. I
[Mr. McMurray.3
believe it has now gone up to something like
42.000.	000 bushels. Of that 29,000,000 bushels, he says that 20,000,000 went to the United Kingdom and about 9,000,000 to the Orient, while for the month of March there were charters for 47 deep sea ships to convey
7.000.	000 bushels to the United Kingdom and
2,900,000	bushels to the Orient. Then he speaks of the export of canned salmon, and refers to the growth of business by export through the port of Vancouver. The hon. gentleman then closes his statement with these remarks:
I am firmly of the opinion that the development of trade through the Pacific portals of this great Dominion will perhaps be the largest contributing factor in Canada's progress in this decade.
What did the hon. gentleman see there? Did he see anything resulting from the National Policy? No. He saw the development of the prairie provinces and of British Columbia by means of a great immigration policy; and I am glad to say that at the present time in western Canada immigrants of a very fine type are pouring into the country from all the nations of Europe whose people came to Canada years ago to open up that part of the country and develop it. To-day the streets of Winnipeg are assuming something of the appearance they had some ten or twelve years ago when these sturdy Canadians were coming in to develop our natural resources. Possibly it was this that the hon. member had in mind in the statements he made. He saw the grain pouring down from the prairies, the coal of Alberta and the lumber of British Columbia being shipped, without the aid of high protection, and all going to develop the Pacific port.
I believe, Sir, that the next fifty years will see a marvellous change in the development of this North American continent. It was natural that those who came from Europe should have settled along the Atlantic coast and in -the vicinity of the inland lakes and the rivers. But in view of the great change which is coming over Europe to-day, the countries of which are impoverished as a result of the war, I believe that the next fifty or, at any rate, hundred years will see a tremendous trans-Pacific trade built up with Japan, India, China and Australia, and then the west coast will see the building of great cities which will be the making of Canada, inasmuch as they will create in our own country a competition in trade between the Pacific and the Atlantic. In my opinion the most desirable thing for this Dominion to-day is to continue that immigration policy which is bringing to the country vast numbers of

The Budget-Mr. McMurray
European people. There are in western Canada 140,000,000 acres of arable land, and with some proper policy of colonization these lands could be put under cultivation so as to produce in Canada the home market which the manufacturers need.
As I said at the outset, I believe that the present budget is a step in the right direction; it is an endeavour to reduce the cost of living in the country and encourage the development of its great natural industries, namely, farming, mining, lumbering and fishing. The only stability which manufacturing possibly can have must consist in cheap manufacturing conditions; without those conditions no sort of artificial barrier will protect these concerns. But with a tariff similar to this that we are considering to-night we may hope to have the manufacturing industry established in this country upon a substantial and natural basis. Coupled with that there should be, in my opinion, a keen searching-out of all sorts of trade with the various countries of the world. I was greatly taken with the address of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) some time ago dealing with the possibilities of trade with the West Indies, and I do not think we can over-emphasize the importance of looking to other countries than those of Europe for an outlet for our vast natural resources. With that, despite the heavy burdens we have, I am satisfied that there is a bright future for this Dominion.
There are some figures which I desire to put on record in Hansard before I conclude. Our Conservative friends have gone about throughout the land telling of the deplorable conditions that exist in this country, but the figures I am now going to submit to the House have something of a ring in them which I think must be gratifying to all Canadians. First of all, in regard to immigration, let me point out that in 1921 there came to this country a total of 100,413 immigrants from Great Britain, the United States and other countries; in 1922 from the same sources we had 70,423, and in 1923, 134,096. This year the increase, I believe, will be considerable. As regards our field crops, Canada's harvest last year reached a total value of $899,166,200. And the mineral production of the Dominion for the year 1923 aggregated $214,019,832, which is 16-1 per cent over that of 1922 and 24.1 per cent over 1921. The figures in connection with our forestry show that for the last 12 months of the fiscal year 1923-24, ending February 1924, the exports of wood and paper amounted to $270,346,000 as cornua
pared with $221,592,000 in the previous 12 months, and $182,207,000 in the 12 months ending February 1922.
Coming now to our external trade, I may tell the House that there has been a rapid increase. For the 12 months ending February 1924 our exports amounted to $1,042,724,670 and our imports $898,338,916. Our exports for the 12 months ending February 1923 amounted to $928,356,656 and our imports $790,032,342; while for the 12 months ending February 1922 our exports amounted to $762,547,390 and our imports $761,026,261, showing a trade balance running strongly in our favour. The exports to Great Britain increased in the 2 years from $293,666,295 to $355,838,316; while the exports to Australia increased from $11,314,906 in 1922 to $20,401,275 in 1924. Our exports to New Zealand increased during the same time from $4,584,349 to $12,541,405. And as for the United States, both exports and imports show a rapid increase, although the former show the greater absolute as well as greater relative increase, the excess of exports in 1922 being $222,905,433. as against $177,580,418 in 1921, or an improvement of $45,000,000 in two years. This is directly reflected in the improved position of the Canadian dollar. In 1920 it required 112.27 cents to purchase an American dollar; in 1921, 111.61 cents; and in 1923 only 101.97 cents. Our railway passenger traffic in 1923 was 9 per cent greater than in 1922, and the freight traffic last year was the greatest on record. The revenue increased by $28,667,000. Our latest information is that for the first two months of 1924-usually the dullest of the year-the net earnings of the Canadian National Railways were $262,376, as compared with a net deficit of $3,270,052 in the same two months of 1923, or an improvement of $3,532,428. There has been a decrease also in the public debt of over $15,000,000. These figures show the present comparatively satisfactory condition of the country despite our heavy debt and the postwar conditions which we are passing through.
I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) that Canada has a great future. And I share the. desires of the people of Alberta and British Columbia for the reduction of the mountain scale of freight rates. I believe such a reduction is in their interest and that they are entitled to it, and that it would set up a healthy competition which would be beneficial to all the western provinces.
During the course of my remarks this afternoon the. right hon. leader of the opposition asked me to explain my attitude in re

The Budget-Mr. McMurray
gard to protecting artificial silk. I have looked up the item. I find that a certain measure of protection is granted to artificial silk. It has never been contrary to Liberal policy, either in theory or practice, to encourage by protection, for a brief period of time, the establishment of any manufacturing industry for which there is reasonable ground to believe that it may be successfully developed. Two years ago I supported the bill to encourage our hemp industry, my reason for doing so being that it was necessary to assist the establishment of an industry that promised to be successful. In Manitoba we produce the finest raw material for such an industry, we have any amount of electrical power and a very large home market. The only factor lacking to the successful establishment of the hemp industry was protection to overcome a large combine in the United States. And so it is with artificial silk. My hon. friend the
Minister of the Interior may have his own * private views upon the subject; but what I have asserted is, I think, correct, and I can find authority for it by referring to some of the most eminent political economists. For instance, John Stuart Mill, who has been quoted before in this debate, has declared that it is reasonable and proper to encourage an industry which has good prospects of success.
I believe that is the view of the right hon. gentleman himself; he stated it in 1910 in that famous western speech of his in much better form than I would be capable of expressing it. With our cheap power, our energetic people, our ample timber resources,
I see no reason why the artificial silk industry should not. be a success in this country, provided it is not handicapped by those protectionist elements that work so grievously against a legitimate industry being established. We have had before us from time to time deputations protesting against the reduction 
of the tariff upon certain manufactured goods, and always the burden of their arguments is that if they were not handicapped by the duty on their raw materials-which were in turn the manufactured product of other concerns enjoying protection

they could and would stand up against any reasonable competition. That is the curse of protection, that it results in the development of gigantic corporations well capable of looking after themselves, and along with them a crowd of helpless cripples economically.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I have great pleasure in announcing my entire concurrence in the budget, which I look forward to as likely to be productive of substantial relief to our great basic industries and to be noninjurious to our manufacturing interests, whom I would not want to see adversely affected in any degree whatever. Not only do I think that our great basic industries will be benefited in large measure, but I am also confident that the great consuming public will be afforded substantial relief.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just to relieve the suspense that possibly prevails throughout the chamber, I beg to announce at the outset that I am not in the Marathon class. I rise to take part in this debate mainly for the purpose of correcting an impression that apparently exists in the minds of some hon. members, and also in the minds of some of our citizens, an impression that has been created during the course of this debate, mainly by members of the Conservative group, who would lead the country to- believe that the majority of the electors of Ontario and of their representatives in this House are protectionists. I would inform the House that Toronto, Hamilton and a few other of our
9.	p. m. industrial cities do not constitute the whole province. For divers reasons we iare changing our opinions in Ontario in connection with the tariff and are gradually seeing the light of day. We welcome the opportunity that our Conservative friends promise to give us in the next general election of fighting it on the straight tariff issue of protection versus free trade or tariff for revenue. We will be glad to meet them on that issue, as we were glad to meet them on it in the election of 1921, when I think the change in tariff sentiment in Ontario was demonstrated by the return of twenty-odd members to this House in favour of free trade. After the next general election we are going to double our numbers on the same issue. For different reasons possibly we look upon

The Budget-Mr. Thurston
the question of the tariff to-day differently from what we did in 1911. Since 1911 the people of Ontario have studied the economic question and the tariff question and they have been forced to the conclusion that a tariff for protection is morally, socially and economically unsound, and the old cry of losing or gaining the home market will have very little effect to-day in Ontario.
I wish to join now with hon. members who have preceded me in complimenting the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on his presentation of the budget this year. In reading over the debates for a number of years past it seems to have been customary for hon. members to always compliment the Minister of Finance of the day on his budget presentation, but I feel that in this case there is an element of sincerity in the congratulations that did not prevail to the same extent in days gone by, and mainly for the reason that the Acting Minister of Finance has brought down a budget that clearly defines the line between protection and a tariff for revenue. The budget was also welcomed throughout the Dominion as no previous budget has been for other reasons, and one was that a good many loyal Liberals throughout Canada from the Atlantic to the Pacific had reached the point of being discouraged and of almost wanting confidence in the Liberal party that had been elected for years on a tariff for revenue or a low tariff cry, and which after it had been returned did not touch the tariff at all except to juggle with it; it did not lower the tariff. And so unless the government brings in further resolutions, a second budget which is often brought down to the House, dealing with the anti-dumping law and the pricing of articles entering this country, which comes under the same law, and in that way offsets the good effect the budget is otherwise bound to have upon the basic industries of this Dominion, the staunch Liberals throughout this country will offer their congratulations to the Acting Minister of Finance with a degree of sincerity that they did not feel in the past.
In connection with the lowering of duties on different lines of manufacture, I should like to take this opportunity of issuing a note of warning to some manufacturing firms in this country. We have been told by a good many, mainly by hon. members in the Conservative group and by Conservative members in the Liberal group that many, many manufacturing firms would be forced out of business and be compelled to close up if there was any reduction in the tariff. Now, I purchase farm implements and machinery of different kinds,
as all agriculturists do throughout the Dominion and when I am considering a purchase and looking over different machinery I always consider that the day will come when I shall probably need repair parts for those machines, and I always ask myself whether the firm manufacturing those implements is on a good sound business footing and likely to stay in business so that I can get spare parts if I should need them; and if I were to see a statement from the Massey-Harris firm that they were going to be forced out of business by this reduction in the tariff I would immediately cease buying Massey Harris implements. So if these manufacturing firms do not want to deal a death blow to themselves they had better steer clear of this "blue ruin" cry over any monkeying with the tariff, because it will act as a club against themselves more than anything else that I can think of at the present moment.
I was a little surprised this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) undertake to tell the farmers of the West just why it was they were in such hard economic circumstances at the present time. It was due, he said, to their careless methods of farming. I wondered as I listened to him, is it not possible that our manufacturing friends, who are putting up the same cry of hard times to-day that the farmers were a year ago, are careless in their manufacturing methods? I think the argument would work both ways. Now as I promised the House, I am not in the Marathon class, and I am not going to say anything more on the tariff except to promise our protectionist friends that when the opportunity does come to the people of Ontario to declare themselves upon the question of protection or a tariff for revenue, we shall be there with the goods.
I want to take up now two questions that are of a local nature, and I suppose if I had followed the custom of most hon. members in this House I would have mentioned these matters upon my first appearance in the House after the election of 1921. In the constituency of Victoria and Haliburton from which I come, we have contributed our allotment to the national menagerie of the Dominion of Canada in the form of white elephants. We have running all the way across my constituency the Trent canal. We can thank both the old parties for that animal. Some have criticized the expenditure on the Trent canal, and I think it deserves all the criticism that anybody can give. The canal should never have been constructed, but the fact remains that it is constructed. We have thrown money into it, and we cannot sell it.

The Budget-Mr. Thurston
We would get rid of it if we could; we would carry it down into lake Ontario if possible. But there it is, and it is up to the government to make the best use of the canal possible, in order to increase any revenue that can be derived from it. Now the only thing the Trent canal is useful for, to my mind, is tourist traffic. For some years back governments have neglected making the slight improvements on the canal that might encourage tourists to come to that section of the country. Now that we have spent millions of dollars on the Trent canal, the only way we can get anything out of it is to bring summer visitors there from other countries and so get the benefit of the money they will spend in our country, and I think it is only wise on the part of any government to remember the expenditure that has been made and to make the slight improvements necessary. An hon. member asks me if it is worth seeing. Yes, visitors will not only see the canal, but as picturesque a country as it is possible for summer visitors to see, through North Victoria and Haliburton and possibly Muskoka; the scenery will well repay a visit.
We also have another beast in the shape of the Dominion arsenal at Lindsay.

I suppose it is simply another example of the wild expenditures that were made during the years of the war. Some people may be under the impression that the construction of the arsenal in Lindsay was a boost to that town. That is not so. Previous to its construction the government of the day agreed with the municipal corporation of Lindsay that if they would carry out certain improvements the arsenal when built would run continuously and employ from 200 to 250 hands. As a result of that promise the town of Lindsay spent practically $77,000 in constructing pavements, laying water mains, and making other improvements. Immediately after the expenditure of that money the arsenal was closed down and has not been opened since, and now the town is out the money that it expended. Discussing the matter with the town council last year, they said that making the greatest allowance they could for the growth of the town from the time the arsenal was built until then the cost to the town through the arsenal being there was 845,000. In the meantime the people have been taxed for

the interest payable on the balance of the $77,000. I should like to recommend to the government that if any opportunity arises for disposing of the arsenal they should take advantage of it. Of course it is unfair for the present government to assume a burden that was left on their doorstep by the previous administration. Nevertheless, I would urge them, if the opportunity ever arises, to dispose of the arsenal to some manufacturing firm, because it is of no use whatever in its present form to the town of Lindsay. It has involved an expenditure of several millions of dollars and will cost a great d*al of money to keep it in repair, it has never yielded a single dollar af revenue to the Dominion treasury. Not a dollar's worth of ammunition, the product of that arsenal, has ever been shipped out of Canada. It has been of no use whatever to the Dominion, and is a white elephant to the town of Lindsay. In all fairness to the town if the slightest opportunity of disposing of the arsenal to some manufacturing firm presents itself I advise the government to seize it.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I have occupied a seat in this chamber for two sessions and part of a third. During that time I have not spoken but have taken every opportunity of sizing up the respective parties represented here. I have one advantage, perhaps, over older members of having had no previous political ties. For this reason I have been able to view the actions of the respective parties in the House from an impartial standpoint, and should now like to give a short summary of my conclusions as to their characteristics. The government party naturally comes first. Until the presentation of the present budget I must say that I was greatly disappointed in the record of what we had been taught to believe was "the grand old Liberal party". They were supposed to represent a party from whom much might be expected; but during the'last two sessions I was convinced that if they were standing anywhere at all they were pretty nearly standing on their uppers. They were shuffling first in one way, and then in the other direction, and it seemed that they would accomplish little. Now I must say they show strong indications that they are going to do something. That is, unless they weaken by not rescinding the order in council with respect to the dumping regulations passed before the bud-

The Budget-Mr. Thurston
get was brought down. I repeat that the government show indications of proving to the Liberals throughout the Dominion that they have some slight intentions of fulfilling the expectations of those who have consistently voted for them year after year.
The Conservatives, the official opposition, must be considered next. I have been greatly disappointed in hon. gentlemen to my left who, I believe, are termed "His Majesty's loyal opposition." To live up to that title they should at some time or other be prepared with constructive suggestions for the better governing of the Dominion, but apparently they think differently. During the time I have sat in this chamber I have not heard any suggestion of a constructive nature from the Conservative party. At the present time I think they are fully entitled to the honour-I suppose they will look upon it as such-of being the opponents of the Canadian National Railways. Their attitude towards the programme of branch line railways brought down by the Minister of Railways has convinced me that for some reason or other they are no longer favourable to the Canadian National Railways as they appeared to be when I first entered parliament, but are now the opponents of Sir Henry Thornton and his board of directors. It is a regrettable position for any political body to take, because if there is any one person in Canada who is making good to-day it is Sir Henry Thornton, and in the fight he is waging he deserves the moral support of every true Canadian citizen. I think too that I am justified in giving the Conservative party a monopoly in the matter of calamity howling and raising the blue ruin cry. We have heard more from them along these lines this session than we ever heard from the famous *"notorious Alberta representatives" a year ago.
I should like to speak for a minute or two [DOT]on the subject of the amendment. I am sorry that in the matter of amendments to the budget we are limited by the rules that have been handed down to us for generations back. For some reason or other the rule in the past has been that any amendment to the budget, whether it be similar to or contrary to the principles expressed in the budget, was a vote of want of confidence in the government. This session an amendment has been submitted by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) which, in subject matter is quite similar to the budget itself; and I think the rule should be changed so that when an amendment similar in subject matter and in principle to the budget is moved, the government would be at liberty to adopt some of the clauses of the amendment. I do not see the sense of submitting an amendment at all, if a vote for the amendment is a vote of want of confidence in the government, no matter what we vote for. If that is the way the vote is to be taken, why all this discussion in introducing an amendment of any kind to the budget? Why not let it go without an amendment and vote yes or no on the budget? That is what the vote means anyway. I would like to see the rules changed so that the government could accept, as an addition to the budget, certain clauses contained in the amendment, or the whole amendment if necessary. If the rules were framed to permit that, I think we would be getting down to the true principles of democracy in allowing the will of parliament to be expressed and accepted by the government.
I propose to reserve my decision as to how I am going to vote on the budget and on the amendment.
Mr. EMMANUEL d'ANJOU (Rimouski) (Translation): Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the electors whom I have the honour to represent in this House, and the great majority of whom are worthy and hardy tillers of the soil, I extend to the government and its able Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) my sincerest thanks and congratulations for having found it possible to present this year, to the country such a praiseworthy budget. After having taken over, in 1921, the administration of the country, which was in such a deplorable financial situation, the government had to display a great deal of fortitude, energy and wisdom to attain such a result. Therefore, it is not astonishing that throughout the whole of Canada this splendid budget was received with praise and satisfaction by all classes of society. The farmers, especially, have reasons to be gratified for what the Liberal government have done for them, and the consumer has the same reasons to rejoice, owing to the fact that the present budget considerably decreases the cost of living. It is, therefore, the great mass of the people who will largely benefit from the benevolent policy of our government. The only element of our population who find fault with the wise policy of the government is the one that has always lived upon and enriched itself through the hardships and toil of our farmers and workmen. The big interests, the magnates of the financial world, the mergers and the trusts, these are the enemies of tariff reduction and

The Budget-Mr. d'Anjou
measures of relief on behalf of the farmers and workmen. They already see, with fear, their excessive and sometimes scandalous profits decreasing considerably, and they are conceited enough to think that they are the only ones 'in this country who are entitled to all privileges, thereby denying to others the very legitimate share of justice to which they are equally entitled.
The government will have well earned the thanks of the country, by championing the interests of the people against the privileged classes. The country has been imposed upon far too long a time by the capitalists. The farming industry, which is the basis of the prosperity of all nations, is granted to-day, by a Liberal government, not special favours, but simply justice. And all true friends of the farming class must rejoice with me and sincerely congratulate the government on such an act.
The lowering of duties on farm implements will turn to the great advantage of our farmers, since it will allow them to purchase at lower cost the necessary farm implements and thereby highly contribute to better, in general, the conditions of the agricultural class.
The first duty of all governments, conscious of their responsibilities is to energetically work in unburdening the tireless tillers who, after all, make up the great mass of consumers and producers. Thus, as the first result of tariff reductions on agricultural implements, the farmer, when purchasing these articles will pay five, ten or twenty dollars less for each and will, thereby, be that much in pocket. Certainly, this is something tangible and appreciable and, no doubt, our worthy farmers will return thanks to the government when the time comes. Whatever may be held to the contrary, the government by lowering the duties on farm implements was inspired by the old Liberal tradition. During the present debate, many hon. members who spoke before me, tried to establish that the tariff policy of the government was not that of the late lamented leader of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The few lines which I shall read, Sir, with your kind permission, will prove, beyond doubt, that the Liberal government by reducing the duties on farm implements, followed in all points, Sir Wilfrid Laurier's policy and that they put into practice one of the most cherished wishes of the great deceased. Thus, in his manifesto to the people of Canada, in 1917, Sir Wilfrid Laurier said:
Should the people entrust me with the administration of the country, I would make it a point to immediately unburden the farmer of all vexatious custom duties. fMr. d'Anjou.]
I would immediately abolish the duties on farm implements and other necessities with reference to farming as requested by the western people. And I would consider as an essential duty of my administration a general and thorough revision of the tariff aiming at encouraging production in Canada and relieving the Canadian consumer.
The budget brought down by the hon. Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is really a Liberal one and the government's policy is certainly in perfect harmony with the idea of the great Canadian who so much contributed to the welfare of his country and whose memory will always be cherished by all Canadians, whatever race or creed they may-belong to.
If we wish Canada to attain its manhood, we should adopt a policy purely Canadian and help by all possible means, the' great farming industry, the first of the national industries; for let us not forget it, our country is essentially agricultural, its future and welfare are entirely based on the progress and development of the farming industry. The crisis we are passing through is serious, very serious indeed, and no one will gainsay that the farmers are those who suffer the most. The United States tariff is so high that our farmers can no longer export their products to that country. This state of things obliges them to sell these products at ridiculously low prices and often at a loss. Nevertheless these worthy sons of the land have obtained these products from the soil, thanks to their unceasing labour and exertions; for, we must not forget, the farmer toils twelve to fifteen hours per day; the eight-hour day is an unknown thing. Consequently, he expects at least to sell his products at a remunerative price. The reduction of duties on farm implements will be of material help since it will allow him to purchase them at a lower price. It will enable him to produce cheaper than he could previously, and, therefore, realize a larger profit on his products. When agriculture is prosperous, the country is prosperous. Therefore, the government will never be too generous towards the worthy farming class, who deserve on more than one score the support and self-sacrifice of all those who love their country and wish its greatness and prosperity.
The balancing of our budget, the surplus of $30,409,000 in our revenue over expenditure shows conclusively the efficiency of the present Liberal administration. This happy state of affairs allows the government to reduce considerably the various taxes which weigh so heavily upon the Canadian people. The reduction and doing away with certain taxes, as well as some changes made to the
