tariff, will contribute in a large measure, to the lowering of the cost of living, and consequently will be to the advantage of the consumer.
Since the outset of the debate on the budget, a great number of hon. members have spoken; very few, however, have seriously touched upon the so important problem of immigration and the exodus of our people to the United States. Yet, in my opinion, the subject is of the utmost importance to Canada, the future of our dear country depends on its immediate and right solution. In the speech which I delivered on March 10, last, on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, I discussed this very important question of immigration and exodus of our people to the United States. Realizing more than ever the importance of the subject, I wish to broach it again to-day, and endeavour to discuss the problem more thoroughly than I did on March 10, last. I would, first, advise the government to entirely discontinue their immigration policy, at least for several years. We have no place in Canada for these immigrants gathered at great expense on the docks of London and Liverpool. Certainly, it is not with that kind of immigration that we shall make Canada a healthy, moral and strong nation. And, while these undesirable immigrants reach our shores by ship-loads, a very sad sight meets our eyes. It is an uninterrupted trek of our people-these sons of the soil-towards the neighbouring republic, in the hope of finding there, the comfort and easy circumstances that their country denies them.
I again state, the problem of the exodus of our people tQ the United States is saddening, painful, even discouraging. In my opinion, the best policy to adopt would be to use all the means and resources that Providence has been kind enough to endow our country with, so as to keep our people at home. The money spent each year for immigration could be given in grants of all kinds, to those of our people, farmers or settlers, who, in a moment of discouragement might feel inclined to abandon the land of their forefathers. Our country is immensely rich in farming land, which only awaits the labour of vigorous and worthy settlers to produce the golden wheat which feeds the world.
How many of those who emigrate each year, sick at heart, would gladly accept the grant of a parcel of land and settle there immediately, with the firm resolve to establish for themselves a homestead and contribute their share to the welfare of the country. Moreover, why should the government . not help them at the outset, which is always hard for these good settlers, by loans on as easy conditions as possible. The establishment of an agricultural loan institution would be a great blessing for our farmers and settlers.
I would suggest to the government to take the initiative regarding such a step. They would be carrying out a truly national and patriotic duty, and greatly helping to stop this exodus of our people to other lands.
To my mind, one of the main causes of this exodus is the Bankruptcy Act. This act should be unsparingly struck off our Dominion statutes. This law has been the ruin of js, great number of our farmers. It has completely destroyed the farmer's ability to get credit, owing to the fact that it prevents our farmer from obtaining the money which he needs to settle his affairs, even at a high rate of interest, because he cannot give the required guarantees demanded by those who are willing to make the loans.	That is
certainly, one of the main reasons of the desertion of our rural districts and the trekking of our people towards the United States.
Therefore, if we are sincere in our desire to stop the exodus of the sons of Canada to foreign lands, we must cut out immigration, help by all possible means our farmers and settlers, either by giving .them lands, or by granting them a bonus as a means of encouragement, or still, by loaning them money under the most favourable conditions possible. Finally we must establish an agricultural loan institution and abolish for ever the Bankruptcy Act which has been so disastrous to our farmers and which has ruined so many of them. The repatriation of our people would be an excellent thing if it was possible of accomplishment. For my part, I maintain that it will always be easier to keep our people at home, if we take the necessary means, than to repatriate those who have departed, and, to give weight to my statement, I shall read an extract from an editorial published recently in the Tribune, of Woonsocket, R.I., and reproduced lately by Le Droit of Ottawa:
There seems still to exist, in Canada, the hope of repatriating the French-Americans. This is a dream that our brothers over there should try to dispel. We do not wish to impose our views, but we are free to think that they would be doing much better by concentrating their efforts on keeping those among them who have made up their minds to depart, by making life at home easier for them.

Mr. Speaker, since the delivery of the budget, very much has been said for and against the proposals of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb). While there is the widest possible difference of opinion regarding the value or otherwise of the changes suggested, there is practical agreement that the government has, at last, decided to eliminate the element of protection from the tariff. Today, once more, the tariff is definitely before the people, and it will be the issue in the election that must be fought in the next few months. On the one side of that contest will be those who believe in tariff for protection purposes, those who believe in pro-

That we realize from reports from all parts of the province that our farmers, especially those engaged in supplying vegetables during the winter and early summer seasons, are gradually being driven out of business by the importation of cheap, field-grown products of the semi-tropical parts of the United States. We therefore humbly beseech the hon. Minister of Finance to help us obtain some relief from these disastrous conditions. The same idea is expressed in the Montreal Herald of March 10th last, in an editorial discussing the increased duty on wheat imposed by the American government. The article concludes as follows:
Even in agricultural and vegetable products we import far more from the United States than the United States imports from us. For instance, during the 12 months ending December last we imported from the United States agricultural and vegetable products to the amount of $78,814,028, while our exports of agricultural and vegetable products to that country amounted to $49,225,234. Therefore, Canada imported from the United States about $30,000,000 more of agricultural products than the United States imported from us. Obviously, the United States is not playing the game, and if there is not a prompt demand for tariff retaliation we shall be surprised. Now is the golden opportunity for the King government at last to give a taste to our Canadian farmers of the benefit of protection. Why should not that $78,000,000 of imports of agricultural products be raised as far as possible by Canadian labour and Canadian farmers on Canadian farms? Putting the question brings the obvious answer.
That is an article from the Montreal Herald, which is advertised as the organ of the Liberal party.

speechtext:
I
congratulate the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Charters) on the excellent address from his own point of view that he has given. With some of the hon. gentleman's remarks I can agree. In others I cannot by any means concur.
In commencing his speech my hon. friend said it could be easily seen that the present government intended to wipe out the tariff. How the hon. gentleman arrived at this conclusion I cannot tell. I think everyone will admit that notwithstanding the changes made by the budget there is a fairly substantial tariff left with sufficient protection to existing industries. My hon. friend also stated that the government has sacrificed the implement manufacturers. I think we can also show good reasons why these manufacturers should not object to the budget proposals and that in reality they are not hurt very much by the changes made.
The hon. gentleman spoke about economy and with much of what he said I agree. He made a statement which I think is deserving of the utmost consideration. It was that a large amount of the money that should be available for different enterprises in this country is locked up in automobiles. I think the general consensus of opinion will be that a large amount of the savings of our people has gone in this direction.
My hon. friend asserted that we on this side wished to sacrifice the home market and thereby seriously damage Toronto and other industrial centres. The hon. member is quite astray in that statement. I do not think any good Canadian wishes to do anything to injure the home market. If I may be allowed to describe the policy of the government, it is that they purpose giving to the dollar its proper purchasing value in order that our industries may flourish, and that those who cater to the home market may receive a fair return for their labours.
The hon. member for Peel stated that he thought it would be only fair to enforce a retaliatory tariff against the United States.
I think the hon. gentleman is arguing from false premises. Why does he not look at the matter in a different light. The United States admits free of duty agricultural implements, cement, coal, boots and shoes, leather manufactures, newsprint, tea, and a large number of other articles from Canada that I will not take time to enumerate. On the other hand we enforce against these articles a high rate of duty. Now, would it not be a more statesmanlike proceeding to say to the United States "We will allow you to send into Canada on the same terms the articles which you admit into your country free of duty;" if that course were pursued it would be only fair in view of what the United States is doing with regard to these Canadian products, or is he willing for the United States to put on a retaliatory tariff on those articles.
I wish to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance on the splendid showing made in the budget, and the fact that he has succeeded in converting a long list of deficits into a surplus. The Prime Minister and the other members of the cabinet are also deserving of praise because they have made it possible for the budget to be brought down in its present form. I think I am safe in saying -apart altogether from what members of the Conservative party think-that the budget will be received with approval by all our people. It will bring a large measure of relief to those who have been looking for cheaper agricultural, mining and lumbering machinery, to those engaged in the fishing industry, and to the consumers of a large number of articles that may be characterized as household necessities. I think our Con-

servative friends, when they are paying their money over the store counter, will be just as willing as the rest of us to welcome the reductions in the cost of articles they buy.
The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) argued in his speech on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne that the government's tariff proposals should have been submitted to the people for their approval. I maintain, Sir, that the people voted on this very question in the winter of 1921, and I would remind the hon. gentleman in question that 180 members were elected to this House to carry the policy into effect. I am glad to know that to-night we are able to congratulate the government in carrying into effect a policy which was advocated by the Liberal party at that time.
Some hon. gentlemen opposite have twitted us with applauding the statement of the Minister of Finance last year on "tariff stability." There is no gentleman in this chamber for whom I have a higher regard than the Minister of Finance, and I regret that he is not able to be with us at this time. However, on the occasion of the budget debate last year I made the assertion-as will be found on reference to page 2,973 of Hansard for 1923-that no matter what interpretation might be placed on the word "stability" as used by the Minister of Finance I for one, and the Liberal party as a whole, would not be satisfied until we saw further reductions of the tariff and relief granted from the burdens under that tariff. To-night I adhere to that statement. However it is only fair to say that if the Minister of Finance had been here he would have presented a budget of the same character as did the minister who acted for him. I make this statement notwithstanding many announcements to the contrary that have been heard.
Before proceeding to discuss the tariff reduction, I wish to refer briefly to the financial improvements as shown from year to year since the government came into power. I pointed out last year where economy should be practised and where large savings could be effected in all the departments, and I am pleased to see that a very effective showing has been made along many lines.
But the members of the opposition state that there is no reduction of debt, that it is visionary and delusive. What do we find? The total revenue receipts are $405,622,760, and the expenditure $375,215,651, showing a net decrease in the public debt of $30,409,109. In addition to that, if our hon. friends refuse to follow the bookkeeping that was established when they were in control of the finances of the country, and refuse to accept their own 
statements, as it were, made up along the same lines as was practised by the former administration, and if they think they cannot discover a surplus, I think there is one way that a financial improvement can be shown. If we turn to the interest tables on page six of the estimates we will see that there is a reduction in the interest of $4,133,592 for this year. This should be convincing evidence that the budget has been balanced, that the debt has been reduced, and that we are having a balance on the right side of the ledger, and should convince everyone of the marked improvements in the financial showing. Last year I pointed out that we had the war burden with us, and no man will deny that statement. With our total war indebtedness standing around $1,693,000,000 and an annual interest charge of $100,000,000 on that account alone we have brought home to us the fact that the war burdens are with us in a very real way. When we realize that our net debt before the war was ogly $335,996,850 and our annual interest charge $12,893,504, compared with a net debt on March 31st, 1923 of $2,453,776,868 with an annual interest charge of $136,000,000, I think everyone in Canada should welcome the good news that our deficits are stopped and the balance on the right side of the ledger. Before the war our pensions were only $311,900, and to-day our pensions are over $32,000,000.
It is'very easy to blame the present government for high taxation, but we must be fair, analyse the exact situation, see where the blame lies and see if the present situation is not largely due to reckless financing of the past government even in the period before the war when they were in office. And if you take into consideration the purchasing power of the dollar now as compared with the pre-war period, the individual taxpayer is paying less for administering the public service so far as the controllable expenditure is concerned than he did in the three years previous to the war; not only that but the late government not only left us the total war indebtedness but failed to meet the ordinary cost of administration for that period, by $13,773,733, and this at a time when money might have been easily raised by various means of taxation.
In three years this government has so reduced controllable expenditure that all our obligations are now met out of ordinary revenue, except the railway expenditure, and the legacy left us in the merchant marine, but I will deal with this later.

. The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
When the Laurier government went out of power in 1911 on the reciprocity issue, one of the cries that helped to defeat Sir Wilfrid was, "Let well enough alone." Revenues were abundant to meet all charges on consolidated fund and nearly all charges on capital account; trade figures were steadily soaring; the immigration tide was still running at the full; every index of national prosperity was buoyant and cheering. There was no Jeremiah in all the land to cast a doubt on the future, no troubles about the burden of taxation, no " Whisper of Death," no cry of " Retrench." What happened in the three short ensuing years? The official records in the light of the present day of reckoning are sadly illuminating. In 1911 Canada's controllable expenditure on consolidated fund account totalled $65,528,512 or $9.09 per capita. With the advent of the new government, however, in the autumn of 1911 there came an immediate change. In 1912, the controllable expenditure jumped to S74,920,944; in 1913, to $85,455,679'and in 1914 to $102,411,415. Worked out on a per capita' basis, this represents $10.17 for 1912, $11.35 for 1913 and $13.31 for 1914. The increase from $9.09 per capita in 1911 to $13.31 per capita in 1914 means an increase of no less than 46 per cent in the three years, of Conservative rule. To use a street phrase this is " going some " and this at a time when economy was imperative, when revenues were beginning to fall, trade to stagnate, unemployment to increase, and cost of living to rise. In 1913, the total revenue was $168,689,903; in 1914 it fell to $163,174,395; and the following year to $133,073,482. In the Public Works department, under Hon. Robert Rogers, who is even now pleading for a return to power of the true Conservative patriots of the pre-TJnion days, the increase in three years of expenditure on consolidated fund account alone was $25,592,413 or over 96 per cent as compared with the preceding three years of the Laurier-Fielding regime. In the Customs department, under the Hon. Dr. Reid, the cost of collecting $100 of revenue rose from an average of $2.78 in 1911 to $4.77 in 1914 or about 62 per cent. In the Post Office Department a surplus of $1,310,219 in 1911 was turned into a deficit of $2,914,541 in 1914. My hon. friend who resumed his seat a few moments ago had the audacity to take the government to task for not returning to the two-cent postage rate. I think I am safe in announcing that the Post Office Department is this year showing a surplus, notwithstanding the tremendous 116i
deficit that was rolled up when our friends opposite had charge of that department.
This was the beginning of our present financial troubles. Whereas in 1911 the per capita amount of our total disbursements on consolidated and capital accounts was $17.03 and the per capita revenue $16.34, in 1914 the per capita disbursement was $24.21 and the per capita revenue $21.21; in other words, the government then in power were piling up our national debt at the rate of $3 per capita three years before the war.
When the world plunged into the devastation of war, Canada, under the Conservative administration was already well started on the path of piling up financial obligations for the uncertain future to take care of. As has already been noted, the controllable expenditure had increased by 46 per cent in three years while capital expenditure had increased by nearly 70 per cent in the face of falling revenues and growing industrial depression. To the present government is left the task of paying the principal and interest on the total deficit of $1,860,113,241 accumulated during the eight years of the war and demobilization period. Now is the present government making its grade back to normal conditions in finance? I wish to submit figures to prove that it is. The struggle has been hard, and that fact is all the more reason why the people should appreciate what has been accomplished, and this is the reason the Robb budget of this year is hailed with delight. I wish to submit figures now for the past eleven months of the present fiscal year.
The controllable expenditure on consolidated fund account-that is for the costs of the ordinary government services-totalled, $132,319,846 for the last fiscal year, a decrease of $8,195,215 as compared with the previous year. Taking the Census Bureau's estimate of our present population as 9,146,457, this works out to $14.47 per capita. It marks the first decrease in per capita controllable expenditures since 1911 when it was $9.09 per capita of population, as I showed at the beginning. In 1921, it was $15.12 per capita, and in 1922, it was $15.68 per capita; but these fiscal years, as hon. members will remember, were both under the parliamentary control of our hon. friends opposite.
Let me turn now to the figures of expenditure on capital account, and the recent record is equally gratifying. Exclusive of the deficits on railways and merchant marine accounts, the capital expenditure in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1923, was only

This brings us to this year with a balanced budget, the first since prewar days, with our exports exceeding our imports for the eleven months by $158,000,000, with our revenue increasing and with our expenditures going down. I think we may look to the future with bright hopes for our country and on the achievement of the present administration with pride and satisfaction.
It is often remarked that out of the large revenue, around some $400,000,000, possibly a saving of $60,000,000 in expenditure is not very much. I just wish to state that this saving of $60,000,000 in expenditure is made, not out of total expenditures, but out of what is known as controllable expenditure, which is very small indeed as compared with total expenditures. The principal uncontrollable items are: Interest on the public debt, $134,258,371; pensions, $34,122,078; superannuation, $1,252,500; subsidies to provinces, $12,375,153; or a total of $182008,113. There are other items due to the war such as Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, Soldier Land Settlement, Imperial War Graves Commission, Battlefields' Memorials, League of Nations Secretariat, adjustment of war claims and so on, which amount to something over $17,000,000. In addition, there may be considered such fixed obligations as those authorized by statute in connection with the Department of Labour, of $150,000 for organization and co-ordination of employment in Canada-see page 51 of the Estimates. Loans to railways for 1921 amounted to $56,000,000 and loans to the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, $900,000. This leaves a balance, as hon. members will see, of $117,971,524 of controllable expenditure out of a total estimated expenditure of $375,213,760.

Yes, for equipment. When you are speaking of equipment, I do not think it is fair to charge up equipment to the public debt, because if I am correctly informed, when equipment is issued, it should be a charge against capital account, as I have said, 'because a lien is taken upon it; and it is an asset that could be turned over possibly for face value for a great number of years, so that the argument of charging up railway equipment to the public debt is not, in my estimation, a fair method of bookkeeping. If, however, they wish to charge up the actual cash advance to railways, it can be shown that the budget then is not too far from being balanced, even when charging up any guarantees or loans clear of equipment.
There is one thing to which I wish to refer, and I am sorry the hon. member for St. John City (Mr. Baxter) is not in his seat. It seems to me that the unpardonable sin that we members on this side of the House commit in the eyes of our hon. friends of His Majesty's loyal opposition is, in the first place, that we will do anything that favours our Progressive friends of the West, and, in the second place, that this government will do anything which will help the ordinary labourer in this country and the farmers in general. The task of our hon. friends opposite seems to be to set the East against the West and the West against the East. I would not refer to this at this late hour to-night, but it is a question that has, I may say, nation-wide significance. Our friends have endeavoured to sow this distrust in the minds of the people against the present administration. They

The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
have endeavoured to make the farmers of the West believe that the government has done and will do nothing for them; that the government did not live up to its pre-election promises; that there would be no tariff reductions or sales tax exemptions. This has been their song during the past two years; we have been accused of not living up to the 1919 platform. It seems to be the purpose of hon. gentlemen to sow distrust in the minds of the people of western Canada and to give the impression that this government is dominated by a voice behind the scenes. We are told that when the West asked for bread the government gave them a stone and that the government was legislating in the interests of the East to the disadvantage of the West. In the language of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter), the government deliberately sacrificed the rights of the Maritime provinces and threw them as a bribe to the grain growers of the West. Now, I think it is only fair at this stage that I should read what the. hon. gentleman said at the time, because as it happened I myself was a member of the Railway committee to which this despatch has reference. It is dated December 2, 1923, and was published in the Montreal Gazette. It is as follows:
(By Canadian Press)
Halifax, Dee. 2-That the government of Right Honourable Mackenzie King had deliberately sacrificed the rights of the Maritime provinces and had thrown those rights as a bribe to the grain growers of the West, was the charge of Hon. J. B. M. Baxter, of St. John, addressing a meeting in the interests of W. A. Black, Conservative candidate in Wednesday's byelection, at Dartmouth Saturday night.. The government had, he repeated, bought the votes of the Progressives with that which belonged to those provinces- and, most, humiliating of all, he said, the sixteen members from Nova Scotia had been a party to the "great betrayal". Not one of them had offered the slightest protest against a. piece of political treachery that had robbed New Brunswick and Nova Scotia of what was theirs by all dictates of justice and national fair dealing, said Mr. Baxter.
"We want men who will present our needs and rights", declared Mr. Baxter, "men-not voting machines".
I do not know that I need read the rest of the article, which is couched throughout in similarly strong language. It goes on to state that the hon. member said the government had the solid sixteen who were voting machines that would support the government in anything and everything, so that the Prime Minister was in a position to deal with the Progressives and sacrifice Maritime rights. That is the sort of propaganda which men who claim to be Statesmen in this country
are disseminating from the Atlantic to the Pacific. As one who was a member of that committee I want to declare right here that in my opinion the prairie provinces had a grievance, for it was shown to the committee that the people of those provinces were being imposed upon by every organization in the West, the banks included; and we believed as members of the committee that in the interests of fair play, between the people of one section of Canada and those of another, the Crowsnest arrangement should be put into effect again. I supported that proposition in the committee, i supported it in the House, and I am willing to stand by it on any platform in the country and defend it. I desire now to put on record a few facts to show just how far-reaching the effect may have been so far as the people of the Maritime provinces are concerned, and the prejudice it may create against the government and the IVest if not contradicted. The hon. gentleman at that time must have known that reductions were given over the Atlantic division which would largely offset any reductions that were made in connection with the Crowsnest pass. True, they may not be as large as we wish or run into as many millions of dollars, because there is not the traffic over the road; but I wish to make the statement that in my opinion the railway management and the government have been as fair to the East as to the West. There has been a reduction of four cents per hundred pounds on ten classes of commodities from St. John, Halifax, and Prince Edward Island to Montreal. Now, I think this shows conclusively that whea that gentleman was making this statement down in Halifax he 
must have known that these rates had been put into effect, and was simply endeavouring to work on the feelings of the electorate in the by-election.
I could quote the Crowsnest pass agreement. I have no doubt that those hon. gentle-

The Budget-Mr. MacLean (Prince)
men who have been spreading this propaganda in the East know full well that the rates in that agreement are more favourable to the East than to the West. A large number of commodities covered by the agreement can be shipped from Montreal and St. John to the West at much lower rates, I venture to say running from 20 to 50 per cent lower than the rates from Vancouver to Winnipeg. So the Crowsnest pass agreement was just as favourable to eastern as to western Canada, in fact nothing would help the manufacturers of the East more than to have those rates go into effect. I do not think it is necessary for me to stress this point, because those hon. gentlemen must be perfectly well aware of the facts, and I can see only one reason for their propaganda-an endeavour to divide the East from the West in an attempt to make political capital out of what the government has done in the interests of the whole Dominion. But our friends have, I think, wasted two years of valuable time. They have been, as the saying is, barking up the wrong tree. They had been endeavouring to persuade the farmers and workingmen of this country that the government was standing by the manufacturer to their detriment. But when the budget was brought down those propagandists woke up to the fact that they must immediately go into reverse gear, speaking in automobile terms, and endeavour to undo their work of the past two years. It is really a pity that so much splendid energy was wasted during that period, for certainly the budget has disabused the minds of the masses as to the direction in which the government is shaping the national policy. One of the best signs of the times is that the government is working mainly in the interests of the people in an endeavour to bring them relief.
In our province the fishing industry is of great importance. I have received a number of letters from my friends there regarding the industry and. asking what is being done for its encouragement. I have obtained a list from the Department of Customs, and after studying it carefully I feel sure that very little further can be done in the way of tariff relief, because nearly everything that is used by the fishermen of the eastern provinces is now upon the free list. Last January the sales tax was taken off all lobster cans, labels, wrappers and cases. In fact, everything that can possibly be done has, I think, been effected along that line. A number of people complain of the sales tax being imposed upon canned lobsters and claim that it should be removed. Under the present regulations the sales tax is imposed only* upon lobsters for domestic
consumption; when the lobsters are exported the tax is rebated. Now, my information is that fully 95 per cent of the lobster packed is exported. Therefore I think the Customs department are only wasting time and energy in retaining the sales tax on this commodity. We have endeavoured to bring this to the attention of the cabinet with a view to the complete removal of the sales tax, but I understand the cabinet regard lobsters as a luxury. But as the government is making nothing out of this tax, whereas its imposition created a great deal of difficulty to lobster packers and dealers, I think it might well be taken off altogether. In the province of Prince Edward Island the fishermen have formed a co-operative union to sell their live lobsters in the States. In the last few years a considerable trade has been developed in this commodity, and it will be largely augmented this year. There is no doubt that those engaged in the industry are proceeding on the right lines in acting co-operatively and sending a man into the American market to handle their output there.
At one time the oyster industry brought more money into the province of Prince Edward Island than any other industry. A few years ago something affected the extensive oyster beds and they were almost wiped out. We have been urging the federal government to clean up some of the beds and reseed them to see if with proper care and cultivation these wonderfully productive oyster areas could not be brought back to their former condition. We hope the government will look further into this matter and give us some assistance along these lines.
Our friends opposite have twitted us because we sometimes refer to railways and branch lines. Speaking for the county I represent, I acknowledge the splendid assistance which the government and the railway management have given us in standardizing the gauge, so that now all our shipments go through to destination without breaking bulk. This wTas accommodation which was long overdue, and on behalf of the people of my county I thank the government and the management of the Canadian National Railways for this great improvement. I hope the good work will be continued. There is a portion of the province where the work is not completed, but I have no doubt that it will be pushed forward with all possible speed.
There are a few matters that I wish to refer to which are of vital interest to the railway, and as the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) is good enough to remain in his seat and listen I will bring them to his attention

To the wharf at Albert known as the railway wharf there was a short spur line from the station, and in the years gone by a large fishing industry was carried on there. Even as late as two or three years ago some five or ten thousand dollars' worth of fresh mackerel was shipped over that wharf, to say nothing of the large trade that may develop in fresh lobsters. A very small outlay would improve conditions at that wharf and give better shipping facilities for the people of that section. The same thing applies to the railway wharf at Summerside, P.E.I. Now that the car ferry is running, on the Borden-Tormentine route the boats have been taken off the Summerside-Pointe du Chene route and the railway wharf has not been used. It is a question as between the Public Works department and the Railway department which should take over this wharf and put it in repair. We have a splendid harbour there, and if the rails are laid again on the wharf and it is put in repair, there is no doubt that it will bring a large amount of traffic for the Canadian National Railways. It would facilitate also the shipment of potatoes and other products from that point. I hope that this matter will not be overlooked. These are really not branch lines we are asking for, but just a little accommodation for the improvement of shipping facilities.
At a place known as Cape Traverse on the branch line to Borden, when the new car-fcrry system was put into force the rails were taken up, on what was known as the Cape Traverse branch and that left the people in that vicinity in some cases eight or ten miles from a railway siding. The roadbed is there, splendid stone bridges are there; the sleepers are there, although perhaps not in as good condition as they were, and the people of that vicinity are asking for the rails to be laid on that roadbed for a distance of about one mile and a half to what is known as Campbell's Crossing. This would allow the people of that vicinity to ship possibly hundreds of carloads of potatoes that are grown by the farmers of that thriving section. [DOT] Another scheme that was under consideration was the building of a branch line to Richmond bay to tap the large mud deposits there. A survey was made of that line and estimates were submitted, and it is asked now by the people of Lot 18 that if the branch is extended to the bay, it be put on the Lot 18 side of the bay in order that it may give transportation facilities to the people in that section who are from eight to ten miles from a railway. I just mention these matters in passing, but I sincerely trust the government
[Mr A. E. MacLean.]
will not overlook them when the time comes for going into them more carefully.
Fur farming in Prince Edward Island and the whole of Canada is a very important industry at the present time, and I think it should secure a little more consideration than it has in the past from the government. The fur companies in the different parts of Canada were formed at a time when prices were exceedingly high, and there is no other business in the world that would have succeeded under similar conditions, but these companies have been able to pull through and are now in a fairly well established position. However, they are very heavily taxed on income and I think that under present conditions this industry which is bringing into the province of Prince Edward Island alone around
11,000,000, a year should receive some encouragement, and we are asking the Department of Agriculture at Ottawa to give us some assistance along the line of investigational work.
Our friends opposite have been telling us that we have ruined the implement industry by removing the protection from the manufacturers. I hold in my hand a little booklet published a short time ago by the Massey-Harris people in which they give some quotations on prices, and it shows that in 1913 a binder could be purchased for 266 bushels of wheat, or S170. Prices commenced to go up and in 1918, with the same 266 bushels of wheat at $1.99 cents per bushel a farmer could purchase a binder for $257 and have $272 left over. In 1919 prices rose even a little higher, but in 1921, 1922 and 1923 the situation changed, and we find that the farmers on account of the very, very low price of wheat had to give 266 bushels of wheat and in addition $138 in cash to purchase that same binder. This table shows how farm products have dropped to such a large extent, while at the same time the price of the farm implements has been soaring or at all events the price has not come down to the same extent as agricultural products. Our friends opposite say the Laurier-Fielding tariff was a proper tariff. Well, for the sake of argument let us say that we had the Laurier-Fielding tariff in 1913. At that time I think the tariff was 12i per cent on farm implements, possibly more, but for the sake of argument we will say 10 per cent. Now in 1913 a binder cost $170, and a duty of 10 per cent gives $17 duty. In 1923 a binder cost $280, and six per cent on that gives a duty of practically the same amount, namely $17, so I do not think our farm implement manufacturers can complain under those circumstances. You will see

The Budget-Mr. Maclean (Prince)
that the manufacturer has the same protection on a single binder as he had in 1913. At the same time, owing to the increased price of a binder the farmer is saved $18.20 duty and a further saving of $16.80 sales tax, making a total of $35.20, which would be the duty and sales tax that he would pay on a binder at $280 under the old tariff of 124 per cent. Now, the present saving on a binder at $280 and a tariff deduction of 4 per cent is $11.20 and sales tax removal of 6 per cent is $16.80, making a reduction of $28. While these reductions have brought great relief to the farming community the manufacturers are not hurt in any way, as the increase in price of their machinery, on which the rate of duty is fixed and collected, gives them the same protection on each binder as they had back in 1913, namely $17 on one machine, and the same thing applies throughout. The high price increases the protection. So I think the argument of our friends opposite with regard to these tariff reductions hurting the manufacturers does not hold water. I see by today's paper that the Massey-Harris Company are fairly well satisfied with the budget proposals that have been submitted.
Before concluding, I just want to say that last year I supported the budget, rather reluctantly. Although I never advocated free trade I did advocate a tariff for revenue purposes, a tariff that would allow the consuming public to import at a reasonable price, and at the same time contribute a certain amount of revenue to the treasury. I stand by that position still, and I claim that the budget this year has got nearer to that point than anything we have yet had in this country.
A train I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister, the Acting Minister of Finance, and the rest of the cabinet upon having brought down a budget which I feel will stabilize industry, will give confidence to the people as a whole, and will produce in Canada in 1925 a boom such as we have not seen for a number of years.
